"""The persona brain: traits and scenario in, a turn-taking speaker out.

The brain owns the composition — how authored traits and the scenario
become a system prompt — and the mapping between the transcript's two
speakers and the model's chat roles. What actually produces words sits
behind the model-client seam, so everything here is tested with the
scripted client or a recording fake.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from egma_simulator.model import CONCLUDE_MARKER, PersonaReply, ScriptedModel
from egma_simulator.persona import (
    OPENING_NUDGE,
    Persona,
    Turn,
    compose_system_prompt,
    messages_for,
)

TRAITS = {
    "personality": "Margaret, 68, retired schoolteacher. Polite but flustered.",
    "language": "en-US",
    "manner": "Warm and direct.",
    "patience": "Waits once before asking again.",
    "accent": "Neutral American English.",
    "backgroundNoise": "A quiet waiting room.",
    "underFriction": "Becomes firmer without becoming rude.",
}

SCENARIO = "Move my cleaning to Thursday. Conclude once it is read back."


def test_the_system_prompt_carries_all_human_traits_and_scenario():
    prompt = compose_system_prompt(TRAITS, SCENARIO)

    for value in TRAITS.values():
        assert value in prompt
    assert SCENARIO in prompt
    assert CONCLUDE_MARKER in prompt
    assert "stay in character" in prompt.lower()


def test_the_system_prompt_has_no_technical_voice_or_model_fallback():
    prompt = compose_system_prompt(TRAITS, SCENARIO)

    assert '"voice"' not in prompt
    assert '"models"' not in prompt


def test_the_system_prompt_is_deterministic():
    assert compose_system_prompt(TRAITS, SCENARIO) == compose_system_prompt(
        TRAITS, SCENARIO
    )


def test_history_maps_to_chat_roles_from_the_personas_side():
    messages = messages_for(
        "the prompt",
        [
            Turn("agent", "Hello, how can I help?"),
            Turn("human", "I need to move my cleaning."),
            Turn("agent", "Which day suits?"),
        ],
    )
    assert messages == [
        {"role": "system", "content": "the prompt"},
        {"role": "user", "content": "Hello, how can I help?"},
        {"role": "assistant", "content": "I need to move my cleaning."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "Which day suits?"},
    ]


def test_an_empty_history_gets_the_opening_nudge():
    """Someone has to go first. When no agent greeting arrived, the persona
    opens — and chat-shaped models want a user message to answer, so a
    fixed stage-setting line stands in for the silence."""
    messages = messages_for("the prompt", [])
    assert messages == [
        {"role": "system", "content": "the prompt"},
        {"role": "user", "content": OPENING_NUDGE},
    ]


async def test_the_persona_speaks_through_its_model():
    class RecordingModel:
        def __init__(self) -> None:
            self.saw: list[list[dict]] = []

        async def reply(self, messages: list[dict]) -> PersonaReply:
            self.saw.append(messages)
            return PersonaReply(text="Hello there.", concluded=False)

        async def close(self) -> None:
            return None

    model = RecordingModel()
    persona = Persona(traits=TRAITS, scenario_instructions=SCENARIO, model=model)

    reply = await persona.next_turn([Turn("agent", "Front desk, hello.")])

    assert reply == PersonaReply(text="Hello there.", concluded=False)
    (messages,) = model.saw
    assert messages[0]["role"] == "system"
    assert SCENARIO in messages[0]["content"]
    assert messages[1] == {"role": "user", "content": "Front desk, hello."}


async def test_the_persona_on_the_scripted_model_walks_and_concludes():
    persona = Persona(
        traits=TRAITS,
        scenario_instructions="First thing. Second thing.",
        model=ScriptedModel("First thing. Second thing."),
    )

    history: list[Turn] = []
    first = await persona.next_turn(history)
    assert first == PersonaReply(text="First thing.", concluded=False)

    history += [Turn("human", first.text), Turn("agent", "Noted.")]
    second = await persona.next_turn(history)
    assert second == PersonaReply(text="Second thing.", concluded=False)

    history += [Turn("human", second.text), Turn("agent", "Anything else?")]
    third = await persona.next_turn(history)
    assert third.concluded is True
    assert third.text
"""The model-client seam: scripted determinism, and a real wire behind it.

The scripted client is what CI runs on — same messages in, same reply out,
every time, derived from nothing but the spec. The OpenAI-compatible client
is the real-provider side of the seam, proven here against a local stub so
its request shape, reply parsing, marker handling, and failure translation
are pinned without a live model anywhere.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import asyncio
import json

import pytest
from aiohttp import web

from egma_simulator.model import (
    CONCLUDE_MARKER,
    GOODBYE,
    ModelFailure,
    OpenAICompatibleModel,
    PersonaReply,
    ScriptedModel,
    build_model_client,
    split_sentences,
)
from egma_simulator.redaction import REDACTED
from egma_simulator.spec import SimulationSpec


def test_sentences_split_deterministically():
    instructions = "Move my appointment. I forget the time! Can we do Thursday?"
    assert split_sentences(instructions) == [
        "Move my appointment.",
        "I forget the time!",
        "Can we do Thursday?",
    ]
    assert split_sentences("no punctuation at all") == ["no punctuation at all"]


def system_and_history(*speakers_and_texts: tuple[str, str]) -> list[dict]:
    messages = [{"role": "system", "content": "the composed prompt"}]
    messages.extend(
        {"role": role, "content": text} for role, text in speakers_and_texts
    )
    return messages


async def test_the_scripted_model_walks_the_scenario_sentence_by_sentence():
    model = ScriptedModel("One thing. Another thing. A third.")

    first = await model.reply(system_and_history())
    assert first == PersonaReply(text="One thing.", concluded=False)

    # The next sentence is picked by counting the persona's own prior turns
    # (assistant messages), so the reply is a pure function of the messages.
    second = await model.reply(
        system_and_history(
            ("assistant", "One thing."), ("user", "Noted, anything else?")
        )
    )
    assert second == PersonaReply(text="Another thing.", concluded=False)

    third = await model.reply(
        system_and_history(
            ("assistant", "One thing."),
            ("user", "Noted."),
            ("assistant", "Another thing."),
            ("user", "Noted again."),
        )
    )
    assert third == PersonaReply(text="A third.", concluded=False)


async def test_the_scripted_model_concludes_with_a_goodbye_when_the_script_is_dry():
    model = ScriptedModel("Only one thing.")
    opening = await model.reply(system_and_history())
    assert opening.concluded is False

    done = await model.reply(
        system_and_history(("assistant", "Only one thing."), ("user", "Done!"))
    )
    assert done == PersonaReply(text=GOODBYE, concluded=True)


async def test_the_scripted_model_is_deterministic_across_calls():
    messages = system_and_history(("assistant", "One thing."), ("user", "Ok."))
    first = await ScriptedModel("One thing. Two things.").reply(messages)
    again = await ScriptedModel("One thing. Two things.").reply(messages)
    assert first == again


# -- The OpenAI-compatible client, against a local stub -----------------------


class ModelStub:
    """A chat-completions endpoint that answers from a queue and records."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.requests: list[dict] = []
        self.headers: list[dict] = []
        self.answers: list[web.Response | str] = []
        self.hold_seconds = 0.0

    def answer_with(self, content: str) -> None:
        self.answers.append(
            web.json_response(
                {"choices": [{"message": {"role": "assistant", "content": content}}]}
            )
        )

    async def handle(self, request: web.Request) -> web.Response:
        self.requests.append(await request.json())
        self.headers.append(dict(request.headers))
        if self.hold_seconds:
            await asyncio.sleep(self.hold_seconds)
        if not self.answers:
            return web.json_response({"error": "nothing scripted"}, status=500)
        answer = self.answers.pop(0)
        if isinstance(answer, str):
            return web.Response(text=answer, content_type="application/json")
        return answer


@pytest.fixture
async def model_stub():
    stub = ModelStub()
    app = web.Application()
    app.router.add_post("/v1/chat/completions", stub.handle)
    runner = web.AppRunner(app)
    await runner.setup()
    site = web.TCPSite(runner, "127.0.0.1", 0)
    await site.start()
    port = runner.addresses[0][1]
    stub.base_url = f"http://127.0.0.1:{port}/v1"
    try:
        yield stub
    finally:
        await runner.cleanup()


async def test_the_openai_client_sends_the_messages_and_returns_the_reply(
    model_stub,
):
    model_stub.answer_with("I would like to move my appointment, please.")
    client = OpenAICompatibleModel(
        base_url=model_stub.base_url,
        api_key="key-under-test",
        model_name="model-under-test",
    )
    try:
        messages = system_and_history(("user", "Hello, how can I help?"))
        reply = await client.reply(messages)
    finally:
        await client.close()

    assert reply == PersonaReply(
        text="I would like to move my appointment, please.", concluded=False
    )
    sent = model_stub.requests[0]
    assert sent["model"] == "model-under-test"
    assert sent["messages"] == messages
    assert model_stub.headers[0]["Authorization"] == "Bearer key-under-test"


async def test_the_conclude_marker_is_read_and_stripped(model_stub):
    model_stub.answer_with(f"Thank you, that is everything. {CONCLUDE_MARKER}")
    client = OpenAICompatibleModel(
        base_url=model_stub.base_url, api_key="k", model_name="m"
    )
    try:
        reply = await client.reply(system_and_history())
    finally:
        await client.close()
    assert reply.concluded is True
    assert reply.text == "Thank you, that is everything."
    assert CONCLUDE_MARKER not in reply.text


async def test_a_conclude_marker_without_words_is_a_model_failure(model_stub):
    model_stub.answer_with(CONCLUDE_MARKER)
    client = OpenAICompatibleModel(
        base_url=model_stub.base_url, api_key="k", model_name="m"
    )
    try:
        with pytest.raises(ModelFailure, match="no words"):
            await client.reply(system_and_history())
    finally:
        await client.close()


async def test_a_provider_cannot_echo_its_key_in_a_successful_reply(model_stub):
    secret = "model-key-must-not-be-spoken"
    model_stub.answer_with(f"Provider echoed {secret}.")
    client = OpenAICompatibleModel(
        base_url=model_stub.base_url, api_key=secret, model_name="m"
    )
    try:
        reply = await client.reply(system_and_history())
    finally:
        await client.close()

    assert secret not in reply.text
    assert reply.text == f"Provider echoed {REDACTED}."


async def test_a_refusing_provider_is_a_model_failure(model_stub):
    model_stub.answers.append(web.json_response({"error": "nope"}, status=401))
    client = OpenAICompatibleModel(
        base_url=model_stub.base_url, api_key="k", model_name="m"
    )
    try:
        with pytest.raises(ModelFailure) as failure:
            await client.reply(system_and_history())
    finally:
        await client.close()
    assert "401" in str(failure.value)

The scripted client is what CI runs on — same messages in, same reply out,

its request shape, reply parsing, marker handling, and failure translation

def system_and_history(*speakers_and_texts: tuple[str, str]) -> list[dict]:
    messages = [{"role": "system", "content": "the composed prompt"}]
    messages.extend(
        {"role": role, "content": text} for role, text in speakers_and_texts
    )
    return messages


async def test_the_scripted_model_walks_the_scenario_sentence_by_sentence():
    model = ScriptedModel("One thing. Another thing. A third.")

    first = await model.reply(system_and_history())
    assert first == PersonaReply(text="One thing.", concluded=False)

    # The next sentence is picked by counting the persona's own prior turns
    # (assistant messages), so the reply is a pure function of the messages.
    second = await model.reply(
        system_and_history(
            ("assistant", "One thing."), ("user", "Noted, anything else?")
        )
    )
    assert second == PersonaReply(text="Another thing.", concluded=False)

    third = await model.reply(
        system_and_history(
            ("assistant", "One thing."),
            ("user", "Noted."),
            ("assistant", "Another thing."),
            ("user", "Noted again."),
        )
    )
    assert third == PersonaReply(text="A third.", concluded=False)

    opening = await model.reply(system_and_history())

    done = await model.reply(
        system_and_history(("assistant", "Only one thing."), ("user", "Done!"))
    )
    assert done == PersonaReply(text=GOODBYE, concluded=True)

    first = await ScriptedModel("One thing. Two things.").reply(messages)
    again = await ScriptedModel("One thing. Two things.").reply(messages)

class ModelStub:
    """A chat-completions endpoint that answers from a queue and records."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.requests: list[dict] = []
        self.headers: list[dict] = []
        self.answers: list[web.Response | str] = []
        self.hold_seconds = 0.0

    def answer_with(self, content: str) -> None:
        self.answers.append(
            web.json_response(
                {"choices": [{"message": {"role": "assistant", "content": content}}]}
            )
        )

    async def handle(self, request: web.Request) -> web.Response:
        self.requests.append(await request.json())
        self.headers.append(dict(request.headers))
        if self.hold_seconds:
            await asyncio.sleep(self.hold_seconds)
        if not self.answers:
            return web.json_response({"error": "nothing scripted"}, status=500)
        answer = self.answers.pop(0)
        if isinstance(answer, str):
            return web.Response(text=answer, content_type="application/json")
        return answer

egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:5:Settled by [Settle the core domain model](.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/01-settle-the-core-domain-model.md), against a survey of 10 voice-testing companies, 13 LLM-eval platforms, the model labs, and the classical testing standards. The frame is adapted from Anthropic's [Demystifying evals for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents) — egma's spine maps onto theirs, with voice-specific additions where their taxonomy has one agent and voice has two.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:9:A **test** describes a situation to put an agent in, and names the **personas** who should call about it. Every test has one home inside its **project**: a **test suite**, the named container for tests normally run and reviewed together. Executing one complete suite is a **run**; each test executed once inside it is a **simulation**, which produces a **transcript**, an **outcome**, and **metrics**. **Graders** read those and return verdicts.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:16:- **project** — a product area inside it: *Outbound*, *Support*. **A permission scope and a query filter — never a wall.** A project isolates nothing; it labels rows so a permission can name a subset and a query can filter to one. Two projects in the same organization are always queryable together. **Tests, personas and graders all belong to a project**, not to an agent. A test has no agent assignment or applicability list, so the same complete suite can run against any selected agent and the results stay comparable. That comparison is the whole point of testing prompt variants, and it is impossible if each agent owns its own copy. Because the project owns nothing, an asset is never *trapped* in one — the failure that forced Humanloop to rebuild its datasets and graders as new object types. See [What is scoped to a project, and what stays at the organization](.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/17-project-versus-organization-scoping.md).
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:20:**The auth provider owns identity; egma owns everything after the front door.** The provider answers only *who is this person and are they logged in*. `organization`, `project`, `membership`, `role`, `invitation` and `api key` are egma's own, and a nullable external-identity column on `user` and `organization` is the provider's entire footprint. egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:26:**agent platform** — the product or framework that runs or exposes an agent, such as Retell, Vapi, LiveKit Agents or Pipecat. An agent platform can offer several connections to the same agent; it is not itself the way egma reaches that agent. A connection can also be platform-agnostic, so its platform may be unknown. Do not call it a runtime: `simulator` is egma's execution system, and earlier records use runtime only for that system. Added 2026-08-09 during the self-hosted phone onboarding grilling; clarified 2026-08-19 during the production-monitoring grilling.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:30:**connection** — how egma's simulator reaches an agent. **Each connection belongs to one agent, and an agent can have many connections.** A LiveKit agent can be reached through its LiveKit room or through a generic phone number; the platform and the connection are separate facts. A connection describes simulation reach. It does not describe how egma receives records of real production conversations.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:58:**persona** — the synthetic person who calls the agent. Who they are: manner, patience, accent, background noise, and how they behave under friction. A first-class, reusable, versioned entity. A persona is either **Egma-provided** and shared read-only, or **Custom** and owned by one project.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:60:**persona version** — one immutable, executable form of a persona. It owns the caller's traits and the complete model selection used to bring that caller to life: LLM provider and model, STT provider and model, and TTS provider, model, voice ID, and speed. The technical voice has no second home in traits or platform settings. Editing any of these facts creates a new persona version.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:62:A persona says nothing about *what* the caller wants — that's the test's scenario. The same persona calls about many different things.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:64:Every project carries one active **default persona** — a project choice, not a persona type. A new project points at Egma's shared default persona. A project may point at any active Egma-provided or Custom persona available to it instead. A default cannot be archived until the project pointer moves. A test created naming no callers receives this pointer, so authoring a first test never waits on authoring a caller.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:68:> Renamed from `digital human` on 2026-08-05 (public issue #8). `digital human` was originally chosen over `persona` for saying plainly that the caller is synthetic — accepting that users arriving from other tools would say "persona" and need correcting. Also considered and still not chosen: `simulant`, `virtual human`, `synthetic user`, `phantom`, `surrogate`.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:75:- **personas** — an array. One to start; several when a scenario should be checked against several kinds of caller. Three personas on a test means running it produces three simulations.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:85:**mock tool** — a project-owned stand-in for one of the agent's tools: the tool's name, and the answer egma serves when the agent calls it during a simulation. The answer may be an error — that is how a test forces the failure branch — and may carry a delay, so a mocked backend takes as long as the real one would. **Matching is by tool name, strictly: one answer per tool.** A mock tool never reads a call's arguments; wrong arguments are caught by grading, not matching, because the arguments are on the record either way. egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:97:**A run pins the versions it executed against** through its evidence records, not through a versioned suite. Each simulation pins its exact test and persona versions, and the run's grading plan pins its exact grader versions. Editing any of them cannot rewrite what last week's result meant. **Authored things are never overwritten**: an edit creates a new version and the old one remains. Mock tools are the single exception — unversioned by decision, and held to one world per run by snapshot rather than by version, for the reasons the Mock tools section gives. egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:101:A run produces one simulation per test per persona. Running the same test twice produces two simulations — there is no separate word for a repeat.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:105:**simulator** — the component that executes a simulation: it brings the persona to life, holds the conversation with the agent over a connection, and emits the transcript, outcome, metrics and spans. It runs inside egma's own deployment, hosted or self-hosted — never anywhere else. Earlier records call it *the runtime* or *the simulation runtime*; `simulator` is the canonical name, adopted 2026-08-03 when the simulator effort began.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:123:**metric** — something **measured**, not judged: duration, turn count, latency percentiles, interruption count, tool-call count, cost. **Derived from the trace's spans by one shared measure module** — the same computation serves the metrics display and the graders, for simulations and production traces alike, so the number on screen and the number judged can never disagree. (Previously *emitted by the runtime*; re-homed to spans 2026-08-14, grader-redesign grilling — the simulator's duty is emitting honest span timings.) Never an entity, never attached to a test.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:135:**grader** — a running copy of a grader-library entry: the row that judges, and the thing verdict rows name. Created by pressing **Use** on a library entry, or seeded at project creation. It points at its entry (`library_id` — the connecting tissue, never null, never orphaned: deleting a referenced entry is refused), carries the entry's `type`, and holds its **filled-in values** — latency's `[{metric, bound}]` — in immutable versions; editing the values mints the next version, and a run pins the versions it executed. Each grader version also points at one immutable grader-library definition version. The prompt or code is shared once at the library layer, never copied into each project, while the exact definition used by an old run stays reconstructable. Redefined 2026-08-19, model-execution cutover; the word previously named the authored logic itself.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:147:**grader library** — the shelf of grader definitions: `grader_library` holds each stable library identity and immutable definition versions hold its executable prompt, output definition, parameter schema, or code. An entry declares its **type** — `llm_as_judge` or `code`; reserved: `human`, `ml_model`, `external`. **Owner derives from tenancy**: null organization and project means egma owns the entry — the one deliberate exception to hard-required tenancy — seeded from a catalog in egma's code. When an Egma release changes a definition, reconciliation mints one new shared definition version and new grader versions for active running copies. New runs pin those versions; old runs keep the old definition through their already-pinned grader versions. No definition is copied per project, and no catalog edit changes the meaning of an old verdict. Team-authored entries land in the same library with tenancy set, when custom authoring arrives. Redefined 2026-08-19, model-execution cutover.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:149:**predefined grader** — a library entry egma owns and ships. v0 ships two: **expected_behaviors** (`llm_as_judge`) and **latency** (`code`). Replaces *built-in grader*, 2026-08-14 — `predefined` is the word users arrive with (Cekura), the persona lesson applied the cheap way again.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:173:**pull / push** — the explicit sync verbs between the egma folder and the platform, on git's model: `pull` writes the platform's current versions into files; `push` uploads and **refuses** when the platform has moved since the last pull. **That refusal is a property of versioned things**: a test earns it, and so do the mock-tool overrides that version with it. A project mock tool is unversioned by decision, so it has no version to have moved — pushing `egma/mock-tools.md` is last-write-wins, and a teammate's edit in between is not detected; the run's snapshot and the answers on the record carry that history instead. Sync is always a verb a developer runs, never a background process — two silently-syncing authoring surfaces are the documented failure (Humanloop's copy-drift).

egma-planning/docs/adr/0002-roles-and-how-a-permission-is-decided.md:1:# ADR-0002: The role model, and how a permission is decided

egma-planning/docs/adr/0002-roles-and-how-a-permission-is-decided.md:45:- The whole model is one table a person can hold in their head, so it is one somebody will actually audit.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0011-one-versioned-platform-api.md:6:Egma's web app, CLI, and outside clients all act on the same organizations, projects, agents, connections, tests, runs, simulations, personas, graders, and verdicts. They use one customer-facing platform API under `/v1`, rather than separate first-party `/api/*` routes and public routes. One executable definition of each operation owns its method, path, request, response, refusals, and authentication choices; it drives server validation and serialization, the OpenAPI document, and one generated TypeScript client.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0011-one-versioned-platform-api.md:8:The platform API covers customer-managed Egma resources, including members, invitation management, API keys, monitoring sources, monitoring import failures, trace reads, and recording access. Identity flows, deployment-wide settings, simulator work traffic, OTLP ingestion, and health checks remain separate protocols. Platform resource paths are organization-wide: a project is a write field and an optional read filter, never a path parent. This cutover changes the contract seam, not the product model: existing resource addresses and operation behavior remain intact after the `/api` prefix becomes `/v1`.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0011-one-versioned-platform-api.md:16:The first `/v1` release preserves the behavior of every current platform operation. This includes atomic agent registration and provider reuse, later connection creation, archive and restore actions, saved test-to-agent applicability, and the current run-selection rules. Those behaviors can change only in a later focused product-model change that updates the contract, server, callers, and tests together. Stable server-owned catalogs remain platform operations in their current form; a screen's private form layout does not become a new resource as part of this cutover.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0011-one-versioned-platform-api.md:18:The platform API is explicit rather than inferred from every Fastify route or every path beginning with `/v1`. Better Auth and Egma's current account and device-login routes stay outside its OpenAPI document. Egma does not add a separate versioned auth contract until a real public account-lifecycle client needs one. Private simulator claim, heartbeat, and report traffic also remains separate. `POST /v1/traces` remains OTLP and is excluded even though platform trace reads use `GET` at the same path; `/health` remains unversioned.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0011-one-versioned-platform-api.md:28:- **Keep one internal first-party contract and add a second public contract.** Rejected because both contracts would model the same platform resources and would drift.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0011-one-versioned-platform-api.md:29:- **Redesign resources while introducing `/v1`.** Rejected because it would mix contract infrastructure with product-model changes and make behavior parity impossible to prove.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0011-one-versioned-platform-api.md:31:- **Generate OpenAPI from every registered route.** Rejected because simulator worker, authentication, OTLP, and operations routes are separate protocols and some carry private data.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-mock-tools-are-served-over-in-room-rpc.md:13:Three facts of egma's own posture bear on the choice. The simulator is already a participant in the room for every LiveKit simulation. The deployment rule is every-arrow-points-out — self-hosters must not grow a new inbound surface to adopt a feature. And dispatch metadata already tells the agent it is in a simulation (simulation id, modality — deliberately small, never the test's content).
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-mock-tools-are-served-over-in-room-rpc.md:19:At session start the SDK reports the agent's tool list and learns which tools this simulation mocks; it wraps exactly those. A wrapped call goes to egma before anything real runs, so a mocked tool's real implementation is never touched. A tool no mock covers runs natively — untouched and unobserved. (Revised 2026-08-09, same session: the first design wrapped every tool so real calls were observed and stamped `pass-through`; the founder cut the receipt — wrapping only what egma answers is simpler, and the record stays honest at the tool grain via discovery.) The simulator's room driver registers the RPC handlers and serves answers from the claimed spec's resolved mock tools — snapshotted at run creation — delaying each answer by the mock's declared delay.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-mock-tools-are-served-over-in-room-rpc.md:23:> **Amended 2026-08-10.** What the SDK actually reads is the identity in dispatch metadata, and one shape of a livekit connection never writes any: on the token-endpoint mode the customer's endpoint dispatches their agent, not egma, so egma is in the room and the agent is never told so. The safety property is untouched — absence still means inert, which is what production needs — but the sentence "no egma participant" describes only one of the two ways a room can be silent, and the other one is a simulation that quietly isolated nothing. Recorded in `mock-tools/issues/04-the-simulator-serves-the-seam.md` with the follow-up it deserves.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0013-test-suites-are-containers.md:7:Egma defines a test suite as an unversioned, named container inside a project, with every test in exactly one suite. This replaces the earlier saved-selector model, which correctly protected test reuse and suite-independent verdicts but incorrectly treated overlapping execution selection as proof that tests need no primary home. Suites never carry graders, targets, or execution settings. A project grader may refer to a stable suite ID from its own scope; that reference selects container membership without moving grader policy onto the suite.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0013-test-suites-are-containers.md:23:A run keeps the stable ID of the suite that started it. It does not copy the suite name, copy its membership, mint a suite version, or store a membership revision or fingerprint. A later rename is visible on old run pages because the ID still names the same suite. Run creation resolves the suite and creates every simulation with the exact test and persona versions it will execute in one transaction. Those simulation records are the execution plan and the evidence; the run row carries no second list of pinned test versions. This is not a version or snapshot of the suite.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0013-test-suites-are-containers.md:65:After that migration, every test requires one immutable suite ID. Do not add nullable transitional membership, compatibility aliases, old API fields or endpoints, dual reads or writes, ongoing backfills, name-based fallback, or legacy/default-suite behavior. Do not preserve the `test_agent` relationship or its filters. The current suite-name-to-run-label behavior is removed. The migration itself is the complete old-data path; product code implements only the new model.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0007-grading-runs-in-its-own-service.md:8:Verdicts have to come from somewhere, and three homes were on the table. Inside the simulator, at hang-up: lowest conceivable latency for simulations — but production traces never pass through a simulator, so a second grading path would exist from day one; judge-model credentials would spread into simulator configuration; and a capacity slot would be held hostage to judge-model latency on every conversation. Inside the control-plane API process: no new deployable — but grading is bursty in a way a request path is not (one run of thirty-six simulations with five behaviors each lands ~180 judge calls at once), and production grading adds a steady stream scaled by the customer's call volume, not by egma's request rate. Or its own service.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0007-grading-runs-in-its-own-service.md:10:Two prior decisions bear on this. ADR-0004 left "how the built-in expected-behaviors grader executes" to the simulator effort — written when the simulator seemed the natural home. And ADR-0005 settled the dispatch shape for egma's standing workers: pull-based claims, outbound-only arrows, zero inbound surface — proven by the simulator in production shape.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0007-grading-runs-in-its-own-service.md:12:The latency requirement that drove the in-simulator temptation turned out not to need it: the simulator posts its terminal transition within milliseconds of hang-up, deterministic graders execute in-process instantly, and parallel judge calls make wall-clock ≈ one model call regardless of behavior count. The judge model dominates wherever grading runs.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0007-grading-runs-in-its-own-service.md:18:**The simulator stays judge-free** and releases its capacity slot at hang-up. **The API process stays free of judge fan-out**; it keeps the grader factory's CRUD and the read surface.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0007-grading-runs-in-its-own-service.md:25:- Judge credentials live only in the control plane's credential store; the simulator's configuration surface does not grow.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-simulation-runtime-is-pipecat-in-python.md:1:# The simulation runtime is Pipecat, in Python, quarantined behind the simulation contract
egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-simulation-runtime-is-pipecat-in-python.md:3:The simulation runtime — the service that plays the persona and conducts simulations — is built on Pipecat and is therefore Python, inside an otherwise all-TypeScript monorepo. Ticket 10 already said "most likely Pipecat"; this record firms it up and adds the reasoning that survived a fresh comparison (2026-08-05).
egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-simulation-runtime-is-pipecat-in-python.md:5:egma's runtime is a *caller into other people's infrastructure*: it must join a Retell session, speak a telephony provider's media protocol, or attach to whatever transport a future connection type demands. Pipecat is a transport-agnostic pipeline whose exposed frame/processor model makes testing instrumentation — per-turn latency stamps, dual-channel recording, scripted interruptions, injected noise, the measured audio band ticket 10 made irreversible — ordinary middleware rather than a fork. The alternatives: LiveKit Agents assumes it owns the media (agents live in LiveKit rooms, adding a LiveKit server + SIP service to every self-hosted deployment) — the right shape for *hosting* agents, not *visiting* them — and its Node SDK, the one TypeScript path anywhere, officially trails its Python SDK. Pipecat has no server-side TypeScript at all, so choosing it is choosing Python.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-simulation-runtime-is-pipecat-in-python.md:9:If LiveKit's SIP stack ever becomes the right telephony backbone, it joins as a transport under Pipecat or as a new connection type; adopting it does not reopen this decision. Licensing per ticket 10: Pipecat BSD-2-Clause, LiveKit Apache-2.0, both compatible — re-check when they land in the build.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-implicit-expected-behaviors-grader.md:8:The domain model required every test to name **at least one grader at write time** — a test with no graders is unfalsifiable, and a suite of unfalsifiable tests is a wall of green that could never have been red, which is the exact false trust this product exists to kill. The rule was sound; its enforcement was impossible. The test factory was ready to build and graders did not exist: no table, no factory, nothing for a test to name. Building a minimal grader entity first would have front-run fog the map deliberately left unresolved (*what a grader is made of* is explicitly unspecified), and sequencing a grader effort ahead of tests would have delayed the simulator's critical path.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-implicit-expected-behaviors-grader.md:20:**How the built-in executes** — prompt shape, per-behavior verdicts, what it reads beyond the transcript — is the simulator effort's decision, deliberately not made here.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-implicit-expected-behaviors-grader.md:24:- The test factory ships with no grader scaffolding and no dependency on a grader effort; the simulator's critical path shortens by one entity.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-implicit-expected-behaviors-grader.md:25:- Every test is falsifiable from birth, and the day the simulator runs its first simulation there is already a judge — no window where results exist but verdicts don't.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-implicit-expected-behaviors-grader.md:27:- The control-plane spec's write-time rejection story ("a test with no graders is rejected") is superseded in place by behaviors-empty rejection; the domain model's test definition and Judging section are edited accordingly, and **built-in grader** / **expected-behaviors grader** enter the glossary.

egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:1:# Domain model
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:5:Settled by [Settle the core domain model](.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/01-settle-the-core-domain-model.md), against a survey of 10 voice-testing companies, 13 LLM-eval platforms, the model labs, and the classical testing standards. The frame is adapted from Anthropic's [Demystifying evals for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents) — egma's spine maps onto theirs, with voice-specific additions where their taxonomy has one agent and voice has two.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:9:A **test** describes a situation to put an agent in, and names the **personas** who should call about it. Every test has one home inside its **project**: a **test suite**, the named container for tests normally run and reviewed together. Executing one complete suite is a **run**; each test executed once inside it is a **simulation**, which produces a **transcript**, an **outcome**, and **metrics**. **Graders** read those and return verdicts.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:16:- **project** — a product area inside it: *Outbound*, *Support*. **A permission scope and a query filter — never a wall.** A project isolates nothing; it labels rows so a permission can name a subset and a query can filter to one. Two projects in the same organization are always queryable together. **Tests, personas and graders all belong to a project**, not to an agent. A test has no agent assignment or applicability list, so the same complete suite can run against any selected agent and the results stay comparable. That comparison is the whole point of testing prompt variants, and it is impossible if each agent owns its own copy. Because the project owns nothing, an asset is never *trapped* in one — the failure that forced Humanloop to rebuild its datasets and graders as new object types. See [What is scoped to a project, and what stays at the organization](.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/17-project-versus-organization-scoping.md).
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:20:**The auth provider owns identity; egma owns everything after the front door.** The provider answers only *who is this person and are they logged in*. `organization`, `project`, `membership`, `role`, `invitation` and `api key` are egma's own, and a nullable external-identity column on `user` and `organization` is the provider's entire footprint. See [The auth and tenancy model](.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/06-auth-and-tenancy-model.md).
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:26:**agent platform** — the product or framework that runs or exposes an agent, such as Retell, Vapi, LiveKit Agents or Pipecat. An agent platform can offer several connections to the same agent; it is not itself the way egma reaches that agent. A connection can also be platform-agnostic, so its platform may be unknown. Do not call it a runtime: `simulator` is egma's execution system, and earlier records use runtime only for that system. Added 2026-08-09 during the self-hosted phone onboarding grilling; clarified 2026-08-19 during the production-monitoring grilling.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:30:**connection** — how egma's simulator reaches an agent. **Each connection belongs to one agent, and an agent can have many connections.** A LiveKit agent can be reached through its LiveKit room or through a generic phone number; the platform and the connection are separate facts. A connection describes simulation reach. It does not describe how egma receives records of real production conversations.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:58:**persona** — the synthetic person who calls the agent. Who they are: manner, patience, accent, background noise, and how they behave under friction. A first-class, reusable, versioned entity. A persona is either **Egma-provided** and shared read-only, or **Custom** and owned by one project.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:60:**persona version** — one immutable, executable form of a persona. It owns the caller's traits and the complete model selection used to bring that caller to life: LLM provider and model, STT provider and model, and TTS provider, model, voice ID, and speed. The technical voice has no second home in traits or platform settings. Editing any of these facts creates a new persona version.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:62:A persona says nothing about *what* the caller wants — that's the test's scenario. The same persona calls about many different things.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:64:Every project carries one active **default persona** — a project choice, not a persona type. A new project points at Egma's shared default persona. A project may point at any active Egma-provided or Custom persona available to it instead. A default cannot be archived until the project pointer moves. A test created naming no callers receives this pointer, so authoring a first test never waits on authoring a caller.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:68:> Renamed from `digital human` on 2026-08-05 (public issue #8). `digital human` was originally chosen over `persona` for saying plainly that the caller is synthetic — accepting that users arriving from other tools would say "persona" and need correcting. They did say it, and the correcting bought nothing: `persona` is the voice industry's near-unanimous term, and now it is egma's. Also considered and still not chosen: `simulant`, `virtual human`, `synthetic user`, `phantom`, `surrogate`.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:75:- **personas** — an array. One to start; several when a scenario should be checked against several kinds of caller. Three personas on a test means running it produces three simulations.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:85:**mock tool** — a project-owned stand-in for one of the agent's tools: the tool's name, and the answer egma serves when the agent calls it during a simulation. The answer may be an error — that is how a test forces the failure branch — and may carry a delay, so a mocked backend takes as long as the real one would. **Matching is by tool name, strictly: one answer per tool.** A mock tool never reads a call's arguments; wrong arguments are caught by grading, not matching, because the arguments are on the record either way. Chosen over `tool mock` because it is the word users arrive with (Cekura, Vapi) — the persona lesson, applied the cheap way this time. Added 2026-08-09, mock-tools grilling.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:97:**A run pins the versions it executed against** through its evidence records, not through a versioned suite. Each simulation pins its exact test and persona versions, and the run's grading plan pins its exact grader versions. Editing any of them cannot rewrite what last week's result meant. **Authored things are never overwritten**: an edit creates a new version and the old one remains. Mock tools are the single exception — unversioned by decision, and held to one world per run by snapshot rather than by version, for the reasons the Mock tools section gives. The run row itself keeps the stable suite ID and no second pinned-test list. See [ADR-0013](docs/adr/0013-test-suites-are-containers.md) and [The Postgres control-plane schema](.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/08-postgres-control-plane-schema.md).
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:101:A run produces one simulation per test per persona. Running the same test twice produces two simulations — there is no separate word for a repeat.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:105:**simulator** — the component that executes a simulation: it brings the persona to life, holds the conversation with the agent over a connection, and emits the transcript, outcome, metrics and spans. It runs inside egma's own deployment, hosted or self-hosted — never anywhere else. Earlier records call it *the runtime* or *the simulation runtime*; `simulator` is the canonical name, adopted 2026-08-03 when the simulator effort began.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:123:**metric** — something **measured**, not judged: duration, turn count, latency percentiles, interruption count, tool-call count, cost. **Derived from the trace's spans by one shared measure module** — the same computation serves the metrics display and the graders, for simulations and production traces alike, so the number on screen and the number judged can never disagree. (Previously *emitted by the runtime*; re-homed to spans 2026-08-14, grader-redesign grilling — the simulator's duty is emitting honest span timings.) Never an entity, never attached to a test.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:135:**grader** — a running copy of a grader-library entry: the row that judges, and the thing verdict rows name. Created by pressing **Use** on a library entry, or seeded at project creation. It points at its entry (`library_id` — the connecting tissue, never null, never orphaned: deleting a referenced entry is refused), carries the entry's `type`, and holds its **filled-in values** — latency's `[{metric, bound}]` — in immutable versions; editing the values mints the next version, and a run pins the versions it executed. Each grader version also points at one immutable grader-library definition version. The prompt or code is shared once at the library layer, never copied into each project, while the exact definition used by an old run stays reconstructable. Redefined 2026-08-19, model-execution cutover; the word previously named the authored logic itself.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:147:**grader library** — the shelf of grader definitions: `grader_library` holds each stable library identity and immutable definition versions hold its executable prompt, output definition, parameter schema, or code. An entry declares its **type** — `llm_as_judge` or `code`; reserved: `human`, `ml_model`, `external`. **Owner derives from tenancy**: null organization and project means egma owns the entry — the one deliberate exception to hard-required tenancy — seeded from a catalog in egma's code. When an Egma release changes a definition, reconciliation mints one new shared definition version and new grader versions for active running copies. New runs pin those versions; old runs keep the old definition through their already-pinned grader versions. No definition is copied per project, and no catalog edit changes the meaning of an old verdict. Team-authored entries land in the same library with tenancy set, when custom authoring arrives. Redefined 2026-08-19, model-execution cutover.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:149:**predefined grader** — a library entry egma owns and ships. v0 ships two: **expected_behaviors** (`llm_as_judge`) and **latency** (`code`). Replaces *built-in grader*, 2026-08-14 — `predefined` is the word users arrive with (Cekura), the persona lesson applied the cheap way again.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:173:**pull / push** — the explicit sync verbs between the egma folder and the platform, on git's model: `pull` writes the platform's current versions into files; `push` uploads and **refuses** when the platform has moved since the last pull. **That refusal is a property of versioned things**: a test earns it, and so do the mock-tool overrides that version with it. A project mock tool is unversioned by decision, so it has no version to have moved — pushing `egma/mock-tools.md` is last-write-wins, and a teammate's edit in between is not detected; the run's snapshot and the answers on the record carry that history instead. Sync is always a verb a developer runs, never a background process — two silently-syncing authoring surfaces are the documented failure (Humanloop's copy-drift).
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:188:| `digital human` | The old name, renamed 2026-08-05 — one entity, one word | `persona` |
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:189:| `simulant`, `virtual human`, `synthetic user`, `digital twin` | Considered, not chosen | `persona` |
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:195:| `caller` | Breaks the moment it's a chat | `persona` |
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:204:The same carve-out covers one more seam, for the same reason: **the Agent Client Protocol names its connection to a driven coding agent a `session`** (`session/new`, `session/prompt`, `session/request_permission` are the wire methods), and [ADR-0006](docs/adr/0006-onboarding-wizard-drives-the-customers-coding-agent.md) mandates that SDK — so the CLI's ACP seam uses the protocol's word as-is, exactly as the auth seam uses the provider's. Added 2026-08-06 after the walking-skeleton code review hit the contradiction. Both carve-outs point the same direction: a `session` is standing machinery you connect to, never the conversation a persona has with an agent.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:212:| `user` | the developer using egma | the persona |
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:213:| `customer` | the organization paying for egma | the persona |
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:220:`trace` and `span` were put on this list by [The unified ClickHouse trace schema](.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/09-unified-clickhouse-trace-schema.md), which needed a word for a conversation that might not be a simulation: a production trace has no test, no run and no persona, so `simulation` cannot name it. A simulation *is* a trace — one carrying a `run_id`. Recorded here 2026-08-02 after a trace-store code review found the ticket's instruction had never landed in this file.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:238:| *(none)* | **persona** | Anthropic's taxonomy has one agent; a voice conversation has two participants |
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:245:- **Thresholds, weights, filters, custom authoring, human corrections, the `ml_model` and `external` types, and any warn tier** — each designed with a named home and deferred, in the grader-redesign spec's future-work section. Deliberately not sketched anywhere else, so the sketch cannot fork.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:247:- **Whether a persona behaves like a real caller**, and how egma would claim it does, is not yet specified. It is the credibility floor of the product.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:248:- **Where personas come from.** Research strongly favours grounding them in the customer's own recordings over describing them from demographics.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-egmas-own-telemetry.md:24:**The simulator is deliberately not instrumented.** Its process-wide OTel provider is spoken for — simulation spans through the ingest door, trace ids derived from simulation ids — and a second tracer provider would fight it over the global API. Its stdout reaches PostHog through the collector like everything else's.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-monitoring-setup-owns-production-ingestion.md:5:A simulation connection says how Egma's simulator reaches one agent. Production ingestion has different ownership, consent, credentials, progress, retry, and failure rules, and a production trace does not require an Egma-agent association. Therefore a project-owned **Monitoring setup** owns production-ingestion configuration. Retell setup stores one sealed account key and selected platform agents; LiveKit setup teaches and tracks OTLP export through the Egma Python SDK. Neither setup is a simulation connection, and platform-specific ingestion meets only at the shared production trace writer.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0010-monitoring-setup-owns-production-ingestion.md:11:Egma was pre-launch when this decision replaced the connection-owned watcher. The replacement deletes old production trace-derived ClickHouse data, old production claims and grading work, watch fields, the webhook route, and webhook state. It does not carry a transition model or legacy read path. LiveKit export uses the existing project API key; Retell Monitoring owns only its sealed Retell platform key.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0002-roles-and-how-a-permission-is-decided.md:1:# ADR-0002: The role model, and how a permission is decided
egma-planning/docs/adr/0002-roles-and-how-a-permission-is-decided.md:8:[ADR-0001](0001-auth-provider-owns-identity-only.md) established that egma writes every permission check itself, because BetterAuth's `has-permission` is organization-scoped and resource-blind — it never receives a resource id, which is structural rather than a version gap. That left the model unspecified: what the roles are, what each may do, and how a decision is reached.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0002-roles-and-how-a-permission-is-decided.md:14:**The competitor ships very little.** Cekura's entire answer is Admin / Member / Viewer plus project assignment — no fine-grained grants, no resource-level lists. Matching that is evidence the small model tracks the market rather than cutting a corner.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0002-roles-and-how-a-permission-is-decided.md:23:- **A named set with an explicit map, not an ordered integer scale.** The three roles happen to nest, so a numeric comparison would work today. It is rejected because **custom roles are non-hierarchical by definition**, and a numeric scale forecloses them. An explicit map is also auditable — the whole model is one readable table.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0002-roles-and-how-a-permission-is-decided.md:45:- The whole model is one table a person can hold in their head, so it is one somebody will actually audit.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0011-one-versioned-platform-api.md:6:Egma's web app, CLI, and outside clients all act on the same organizations, projects, agents, connections, tests, runs, simulations, personas, graders, and verdicts. They use one customer-facing platform API under `/v1`, rather than separate first-party `/api/*` routes and public routes. One executable definition of each operation owns its method, path, request, response, refusals, and authentication choices; it drives server validation and serialization, the OpenAPI document, and one generated TypeScript client.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0011-one-versioned-platform-api.md:8:The platform API covers customer-managed Egma resources, including members, invitation management, API keys, monitoring sources, monitoring import failures, trace reads, and recording access. Identity flows, deployment-wide settings, simulator work traffic, OTLP ingestion, and health checks remain separate protocols. Platform resource paths are organization-wide: a project is a write field and an optional read filter, never a path parent. This cutover changes the contract seam, not the product model: existing resource addresses and operation behavior remain intact after the `/api` prefix becomes `/v1`.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0011-one-versioned-platform-api.md:16:The first `/v1` release preserves the behavior of every current platform operation. This includes atomic agent registration and provider reuse, later connection creation, archive and restore actions, saved test-to-agent applicability, and the current run-selection rules. Those behaviors can change only in a later focused product-model change that updates the contract, server, callers, and tests together. Stable server-owned catalogs remain platform operations in their current form; a screen's private form layout does not become a new resource as part of this cutover.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0011-one-versioned-platform-api.md:18:The platform API is explicit rather than inferred from every Fastify route or every path beginning with `/v1`. Better Auth and Egma's current account and device-login routes stay outside its OpenAPI document. Egma does not add a separate versioned auth contract until a real public account-lifecycle client needs one. Private simulator claim, heartbeat, and report traffic also remains separate. `POST /v1/traces` remains OTLP and is excluded even though platform trace reads use `GET` at the same path; `/health` remains unversioned.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0011-one-versioned-platform-api.md:28:- **Keep one internal first-party contract and add a second public contract.** Rejected because both contracts would model the same platform resources and would drift.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0011-one-versioned-platform-api.md:29:- **Redesign resources while introducing `/v1`.** Rejected because it would mix contract infrastructure with product-model changes and make behavior parity impossible to prove.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0011-one-versioned-platform-api.md:31:- **Generate OpenAPI from every registered route.** Rejected because simulator worker, authentication, OTLP, and operations routes are separate protocols and some carry private data.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-mock-tools-are-served-over-in-room-rpc.md:13:Three facts of egma's own posture bear on the choice. The simulator is already a participant in the room for every LiveKit simulation. The deployment rule is every-arrow-points-out — self-hosters must not grow a new inbound surface to adopt a feature. And dispatch metadata already tells the agent it is in a simulation (simulation id, modality — deliberately small, never the test's content).
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-mock-tools-are-served-over-in-room-rpc.md:19:At session start the SDK reports the agent's tool list and learns which tools this simulation mocks; it wraps exactly those. A wrapped call goes to egma before anything real runs, so a mocked tool's real implementation is never touched. A tool no mock covers runs natively — untouched and unobserved. (Revised 2026-08-09, same session: the first design wrapped every tool so real calls were observed and stamped `pass-through`; the founder cut the receipt — wrapping only what egma answers is simpler, and the record stays honest at the tool grain via discovery.) The simulator's room driver registers the RPC handlers and serves answers from the claimed spec's resolved mock tools — snapshotted at run creation — delaying each answer by the mock's declared delay.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-mock-tools-are-served-over-in-room-rpc.md:23:> **Amended 2026-08-10.** What the SDK actually reads is the identity in dispatch metadata, and one shape of a livekit connection never writes any: on the token-endpoint mode the customer's endpoint dispatches their agent, not egma, so egma is in the room and the agent is never told so. The safety property is untouched — absence still means inert, which is what production needs — but the sentence "no egma participant" describes only one of the two ways a room can be silent, and the other one is a simulation that quietly isolated nothing. Recorded in `mock-tools/issues/04-the-simulator-serves-the-seam.md` with the follow-up it deserves.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0013-test-suites-are-containers.md:7:Egma defines a test suite as an unversioned, named container inside a project, with every test in exactly one suite. This replaces the earlier saved-selector model, which correctly protected test reuse and suite-independent verdicts but incorrectly treated overlapping execution selection as proof that tests need no primary home. Suites never carry graders, targets, or execution settings. A project grader may refer to a stable suite ID from its own scope; that reference selects container membership without moving grader policy onto the suite.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0013-test-suites-are-containers.md:23:A run keeps the stable ID of the suite that started it. It does not copy the suite name, copy its membership, mint a suite version, or store a membership revision or fingerprint. A later rename is visible on old run pages because the ID still names the same suite. Run creation resolves the suite and creates every simulation with the exact test and persona versions it will execute in one transaction. Those simulation records are the execution plan and the evidence; the run row carries no second list of pinned test versions. This is not a version or snapshot of the suite.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0013-test-suites-are-containers.md:65:After that migration, every test requires one immutable suite ID. Do not add nullable transitional membership, compatibility aliases, old API fields or endpoints, dual reads or writes, ongoing backfills, name-based fallback, or legacy/default-suite behavior. Inside the control-plane API process: no new deployable — but grading is bursty in a way a request path is not (one run of thirty-six simulations with five behaviors each lands ~180 judge calls at once), and production grading adds a steady stream scaled by the customer's call volume, not by egma's request rate. egma-planning/docs/adr/0007-grading-runs-in-its-own-service.md:10:Two prior decisions bear on this. egma-planning/docs/adr/0007-grading-runs-in-its-own-service.md:18:**The simulator stays judge-free** and releases its capacity slot at hang-up. **The API process stays free of judge fan-out**; it keeps the grader factory's CRUD and the read surface.

egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-simulation-runtime-is-pipecat-in-python.md:1:# The simulation runtime is Pipecat, in Python, quarantined behind the simulation contract
egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-simulation-runtime-is-pipecat-in-python.md:3:The simulation runtime — the service that plays the persona and conducts simulations — is built on Pipecat and is therefore Python, inside an otherwise all-TypeScript monorepo. Ticket 10 already said "most likely Pipecat"; this record firms it up and adds the reasoning that survived a fresh comparison (2026-08-05).
egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-simulation-runtime-is-pipecat-in-python.md:5:egma's runtime is a *caller into other people's infrastructure*: it must join a Retell session, speak a telephony provider's media protocol, or attach to whatever transport a future connection type demands. Pipecat is a transport-agnostic pipeline whose exposed frame/processor model makes testing instrumentation — per-turn latency stamps, dual-channel recording, scripted interruptions, injected noise, the measured audio band ticket 10 made irreversible — ordinary middleware rather than a fork. The alternatives: LiveKit Agents assumes it owns the media (agents live in LiveKit rooms, adding a LiveKit server + SIP service to every self-hosted deployment) — the right shape for *hosting* agents, not *visiting* them — and its Node SDK, the one TypeScript path anywhere, officially trails its Python SDK. egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-simulation-runtime-is-pipecat-in-python.md:9:If LiveKit's SIP stack ever becomes the right telephony backbone, it joins as a transport under Pipecat or as a new connection type; adopting it does not reopen this decision. egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-implicit-expected-behaviors-grader.md:8:The domain model required every test to name **at least one grader at write time** — a test with no graders is unfalsifiable, and a suite of unfalsifiable tests is a wall of green that could never have been red, which is the exact false trust this product exists to kill. Building a minimal grader entity first would have front-run fog the map deliberately left unresolved (*what a grader is made of* is explicitly unspecified), and sequencing a grader effort ahead of tests would have delayed the simulator's critical path.

egma-planning/docs/adr/0009-the-cli-and-the-platform-ship-together.md:16:Ticket 08 makes the coupling tighter rather than looser. The repository file format now records a behavior's priority, a persona's stable identifier, a test's description, its graders, its required capabilities, and the identity revision of its live half. A CLI that cannot read those cannot write a correct file, and a platform that cannot answer them cannot be written to correctly.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0009-the-cli-and-the-platform-ship-together.md:25:- The number is bumped whenever a shape a repository client reads or writes changes. Contract **2** was: behaviors carry a priority, personas carry a stable identifier beside their display name, a test carries a description, graders, required capabilities and an identity revision, and a repository write names both the version and the revision it was written against.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0009-the-cli-and-the-platform-ship-together.md:26:- **Contract 3 is the current one, and it is the first bump this decision was written to absorb.** The grader redesign ([ADR-0009 on graders](0009-grader-library-and-running-copies.md), 2026-08-14) retired the two fields contract 2 was mostly defined by: an expected behavior is a plain sentence again, because under binary scoring every behavior must hold and a priority had nothing left to say; and a test names no graders, because the project's running copies judge every test and the junction is dropped. Contract 3 is contract 2 without those two — a persona's stable identifier, a test's description, its required capabilities, its identity revision, and a write naming both the version and the revision. On read, a contract-2 file is tolerated rather than refused: the `[P0]` markers and the `graders:` key are passed over and the file is rewritten as contract 3. That tolerance is deliberate and it is the one place this decision bends, because refusing would strand a folder somebody committed months ago over fields the platform has stopped having an opinion about.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0014-object-storage-is-the-trace-ingestion-boundary.md:6:Egma is pre-production, so this is one forward replacement rather than a compatibility migration. The existing OTLP wire contract and `POST /v1/traces` URL remain unchanged. Customer production OTLP and simulator service-token OTLP use the same ingestion path; Retell enters it through the same internal acceptance module. Egma authenticates, validates, and normalizes accepted evidence, appends the versioned normalized envelope to a bounded local staging write-ahead log, and groups those records into immutable segments. It uploads each segment to the configured object store: AWS S3 for hosted Egma and MinIO for self-hosted Egma.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0014-object-storage-is-the-trace-ingestion-boundary.md:36:Evidence content is preserved. Egma does not scan or rewrite transcript text, tool arguments or results, metadata, PII, or arbitrary fields whose names or values look credential-like. Request authorization, the simulator service token, configured Retell key, and object-store credentials stay outside evidence by construction. The first Retell evidence contract omits only its top-level `access_token` and values for the exact case-insensitive header names `authorization`, `proxy-authorization`, `cookie`, `set-cookie`, `api-key`, and `x-api-key` inside Retell's named `custom_sip_headers` map. Egma omits those exact fields; it does not insert redaction text. A future omission requires an explicit versioned evidence-contract change and round-trip proof rather than a new heuristic.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0001-auth-provider-owns-identity-only.md:9:`architecture.md` locks BetterAuth for authentication, and one codebase must serve both self-hosters and an egma-run cloud service. A standing constraint from [The auth and tenancy model](../../.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/06-auth-and-tenancy-model.md) adds a third requirement: auth must sit behind an interface narrow enough that WorkOS could replace BetterAuth for the cloud service later without touching the rest of the codebase.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0001-auth-provider-owns-identity-only.md:11:BetterAuth ships an organization plugin (organization → team → member, with roles and invitations) and an API-key plugin. Adopting them would save real work. The question is whether the identity library should also model egma's tenancy.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0001-auth-provider-owns-identity-only.md:17:**No hosted vendor can own tenancy for an open-source product.** Auth0 and Clerk both ship "Organizations" and both are cloud-only. A self-hoster could not run egma if its org model lived there. The same reasoning already ruled out WorkOS FGA, which is hosted-only.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0001-auth-provider-owns-identity-only.md:34:  > **Corrected 2026-08-01.** This bullet previously read *"the provider sits on the login path only, never the authenticated-request path."* That is false as written — BetterAuth validates the session cookie on every browser request. The following clause (*"once a request carries an egma API key"*) scoped it correctly, but the headline sentence was read on its own and misled. The same phrasing appeared in the map's standing notes and has been corrected there too, because those notes are read at the start of every session rather than being a record of one. [Ticket 06](../../.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/06-auth-and-tenancy-model.md) keeps the original wording and is left alone: a resolved ticket is the history of a decision, not live guidance.

egma-planning/docs/adr/0001-auth-provider-owns-identity-only.md:72:So a swap needs **no data migration and no re-modelling**. Nothing is exported from a vendor, nothing is re-keyed, no row moves. That was the half that could have cost a quarter, and it is safe. Nothing below takes it back.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0001-auth-provider-owns-identity-only.md:97:**Days of work, in files that are already listed. Not a migration, not a re-model, not a data risk.** The failure mode is a login page that stops working until it is fixed, which is loud, local and testable — not a silent tenancy bug, which is the class this whole design was built to make impossible.
