egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:1:# Domain model
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:5:Settled by [Settle the core domain model](.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/01-settle-the-core-domain-model.md), against a survey of 10 voice-testing companies, 13 LLM-eval platforms, the model labs, and the classical testing standards. The frame is adapted from Anthropic's [Demystifying evals for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents) — egma's spine maps onto theirs, with voice-specific additions where their taxonomy has one agent and voice has two.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:9:A **test** describes a situation to put an agent in, and names the **personas** who should call about it. Every test has one home inside its **project**: a **test suite**, the named container for tests normally run and reviewed together. Executing one complete suite is a **run**; each test executed once inside it is a **simulation**, which produces a **transcript**, an **outcome**, and **metrics**. **Graders** read those and return verdicts.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:16:- **project** — a product area inside it: *Outbound*, *Support*. **A permission scope and a query filter — never a wall.** A project isolates nothing; it labels rows so a permission can name a subset and a query can filter to one. Two projects in the same organization are always queryable together. **Tests, personas and graders all belong to a project**, not to an agent. A test has no agent assignment or applicability list, so the same complete suite can run against any selected agent and the results stay comparable. That comparison is the whole point of testing prompt variants, and it is impossible if each agent owns its own copy. Because the project owns nothing, an asset is never *trapped* in one — the failure that forced Humanloop to rebuild its datasets and graders as new object types. See [What is scoped to a project, and what stays at the organization](.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/17-project-versus-organization-scoping.md).
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:20:**The auth provider owns identity; egma owns everything after the front door.** The provider answers only *who is this person and are they logged in*. `organization`, `project`, `membership`, `role`, `invitation` and `api key` are egma's own, and a nullable external-identity column on `user` and `organization` is the provider's entire footprint. See [The auth and tenancy model](.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/06-auth-and-tenancy-model.md).
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:26:**agent platform** — the product or framework that runs or exposes an agent, such as Retell, Vapi, LiveKit Agents or Pipecat. An agent platform can offer several connections to the same agent; it is not itself the way egma reaches that agent. A connection can also be platform-agnostic, so its platform may be unknown. Do not call it a runtime: `simulator` is egma's execution system, and earlier records use runtime only for that system. Added 2026-08-09 during the self-hosted phone onboarding grilling; clarified 2026-08-19 during the production-monitoring grilling.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:30:**connection** — how egma's simulator reaches an agent. **Each connection belongs to one agent, and an agent can have many connections.** A LiveKit agent can be reached through its LiveKit room or through a generic phone number; the platform and the connection are separate facts. A connection describes simulation reach. It does not describe how egma receives records of real production conversations.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:58:**persona** — the synthetic person who calls the agent. Who they are: manner, patience, accent, background noise, and how they behave under friction. A first-class, reusable, versioned entity. A persona is either **Egma-provided** and shared read-only, or **Custom** and owned by one project.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:60:**persona version** — one immutable, executable form of a persona. It owns the caller's traits and the complete model selection used to bring that caller to life: LLM provider and model, STT provider and model, and TTS provider, model, voice ID, and speed. The technical voice has no second home in traits or platform settings. Editing any of these facts creates a new persona version.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:62:A persona says nothing about *what* the caller wants — that's the test's scenario. The same persona calls about many different things.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:64:Every project carries one active **default persona** — a project choice, not a persona type. A new project points at Egma's shared default persona. A project may point at any active Egma-provided or Custom persona available to it instead. A default cannot be archived until the project pointer moves. A test created naming no callers receives this pointer, so authoring a first test never waits on authoring a caller.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:68:> Renamed from `digital human` on 2026-08-05 (public issue #8). `digital human` was originally chosen over `persona` for saying plainly that the caller is synthetic — accepting that users arriving from other tools would say "persona" and need correcting. They did say it, and the correcting bought nothing: `persona` is the voice industry's near-unanimous term, and now it is egma's. Also considered and still not chosen: `simulant`, `virtual human`, `synthetic user`, `phantom`, `surrogate`.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:75:- **personas** — an array. One to start; several when a scenario should be checked against several kinds of caller. Three personas on a test means running it produces three simulations.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:85:**mock tool** — a project-owned stand-in for one of the agent's tools: the tool's name, and the answer egma serves when the agent calls it during a simulation. The answer may be an error — that is how a test forces the failure branch — and may carry a delay, so a mocked backend takes as long as the real one would. **Matching is by tool name, strictly: one answer per tool.** A mock tool never reads a call's arguments; wrong arguments are caught by grading, not matching, because the arguments are on the record either way. Chosen over `tool mock` because it is the word users arrive with (Cekura, Vapi) — the persona lesson, applied the cheap way this time. Added 2026-08-09, mock-tools grilling.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:97:**A run pins the versions it executed against** through its evidence records, not through a versioned suite. Each simulation pins its exact test and persona versions, and the run's grading plan pins its exact grader versions. Editing any of them cannot rewrite what last week's result meant. **Authored things are never overwritten**: an edit creates a new version and the old one remains. Mock tools are the single exception — unversioned by decision, and held to one world per run by snapshot rather than by version, for the reasons the Mock tools section gives. The run row itself keeps the stable suite ID and no second pinned-test list. See [ADR-0013](docs/adr/0013-test-suites-are-containers.md) and [The Postgres control-plane schema](.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/08-postgres-control-plane-schema.md).
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:101:A run produces one simulation per test per persona. Running the same test twice produces two simulations — there is no separate word for a repeat.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:105:**simulator** — the component that executes a simulation: it brings the persona to life, holds the conversation with the agent over a connection, and emits the transcript, outcome, metrics and spans. It runs inside egma's own deployment, hosted or self-hosted — never anywhere else. Earlier records call it *the runtime* or *the simulation runtime*; `simulator` is the canonical name, adopted 2026-08-03 when the simulator effort began.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:123:**metric** — something **measured**, not judged: duration, turn count, latency percentiles, interruption count, tool-call count, cost. **Derived from the trace's spans by one shared measure module** — the same computation serves the metrics display and the graders, for simulations and production traces alike, so the number on screen and the number judged can never disagree. (Previously *emitted by the runtime*; re-homed to spans 2026-08-14, grader-redesign grilling — the simulator's duty is emitting honest span timings.) Never an entity, never attached to a test.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:135:**grader** — a running copy of a grader-library entry: the row that judges, and the thing verdict rows name. Created by pressing **Use** on a library entry, or seeded at project creation. It points at its entry (`library_id` — the connecting tissue, never null, never orphaned: deleting a referenced entry is refused), carries the entry's `type`, and holds its **filled-in values** — latency's `[{metric, bound}]` — in immutable versions; editing the values mints the next version, and a run pins the versions it executed. Each grader version also points at one immutable grader-library definition version. The prompt or code is shared once at the library layer, never copied into each project, while the exact definition used by an old run stays reconstructable. Redefined 2026-08-19, model-execution cutover; the word previously named the authored logic itself.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:147:**grader library** — the shelf of grader definitions: `grader_library` holds each stable library identity and immutable definition versions hold its executable prompt, output definition, parameter schema, or code. An entry declares its **type** — `llm_as_judge` or `code`; reserved: `human`, `ml_model`, `external`. **Owner derives from tenancy**: null organization and project means egma owns the entry — the one deliberate exception to hard-required tenancy — seeded from a catalog in egma's code. When an Egma release changes a definition, reconciliation mints one new shared definition version and new grader versions for active running copies. New runs pin those versions; old runs keep the old definition through their already-pinned grader versions. No definition is copied per project, and no catalog edit changes the meaning of an old verdict. Team-authored entries land in the same library with tenancy set, when custom authoring arrives. Redefined 2026-08-19, model-execution cutover.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:149:**predefined grader** — a library entry egma owns and ships. v0 ships two: **expected_behaviors** (`llm_as_judge`) and **latency** (`code`). Replaces *built-in grader*, 2026-08-14 — `predefined` is the word users arrive with (Cekura), the persona lesson applied the cheap way again.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:173:**pull / push** — the explicit sync verbs between the egma folder and the platform, on git's model: `pull` writes the platform's current versions into files; `push` uploads and **refuses** when the platform has moved since the last pull. **That refusal is a property of versioned things**: a test earns it, and so do the mock-tool overrides that version with it. A project mock tool is unversioned by decision, so it has no version to have moved — pushing `egma/mock-tools.md` is last-write-wins, and a teammate's edit in between is not detected; the run's snapshot and the answers on the record carry that history instead. Sync is always a verb a developer runs, never a background process — two silently-syncing authoring surfaces are the documented failure (Humanloop's copy-drift).

egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:1:# Domain model
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:5:Settled by [Settle the core domain model](.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/01-settle-the-core-domain-model.md), against a survey of 10 voice-testing companies, 13 LLM-eval platforms, the model labs, and the classical testing standards. The frame is adapted from Anthropic's [Demystifying evals for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents) — egma's spine maps onto theirs, with voice-specific additions where their taxonomy has one agent and voice has two.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:9:A **test** describes a situation to put an agent in, and names the **personas** who should call about it. Every test has one home inside its **project**: a **test suite**, the named container for tests normally run and reviewed together. Executing one complete suite is a **run**; each test executed once inside it is a **simulation**, which produces a **transcript**, an **outcome**, and **metrics**. **Graders** read those and return verdicts.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:16:- **project** — a product area inside it: *Outbound*, *Support*. **A permission scope and a query filter — never a wall.** A project isolates nothing; it labels rows so a permission can name a subset and a query can filter to one. Two projects in the same organization are always queryable together. **Tests, personas and graders all belong to a project**, not to an agent. A test has no agent assignment or applicability list, so the same complete suite can run against any selected agent and the results stay comparable. That comparison is the whole point of testing prompt variants, and it is impossible if each agent owns its own copy. Because the project owns nothing, an asset is never *trapped* in one — the failure that forced Humanloop to rebuild its datasets and graders as new object types. See [What is scoped to a project, and what stays at the organization](.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/17-project-versus-organization-scoping.md).
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:20:**The auth provider owns identity; egma owns everything after the front door.** The provider answers only *who is this person and are they logged in*. `organization`, `project`, `membership`, `role`, `invitation` and `api key` are egma's own, and a nullable external-identity column on `user` and `organization` is the provider's entire footprint. See [The auth and tenancy model](.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/06-auth-and-tenancy-model.md).
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:26:**agent platform** — the product or framework that runs or exposes an agent, such as Retell, Vapi, LiveKit Agents or Pipecat. An agent platform can offer several connections to the same agent; it is not itself the way egma reaches that agent. A connection can also be platform-agnostic, so its platform may be unknown. Do not call it a runtime: `simulator` is egma's execution system, and earlier records use runtime only for that system. Added 2026-08-09 during the self-hosted phone onboarding grilling; clarified 2026-08-19 during the production-monitoring grilling.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:30:**connection** — how egma's simulator reaches an agent. **Each connection belongs to one agent, and an agent can have many connections.** A LiveKit agent can be reached through its LiveKit room or through a generic phone number; the platform and the connection are separate facts. A connection describes simulation reach. It does not describe how egma receives records of real production conversations.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:58:**persona** — the synthetic person who calls the agent. Who they are: manner, patience, accent, background noise, and how they behave under friction. A first-class, reusable, versioned entity. A persona is either **Egma-provided** and shared read-only, or **Custom** and owned by one project.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:60:**persona version** — one immutable, executable form of a persona. It owns the caller's traits and the complete model selection used to bring that caller to life: LLM provider and model, STT provider and model, and TTS provider, model, voice ID, and speed. The technical voice has no second home in traits or platform settings. Editing any of these facts creates a new persona version.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:62:A persona says nothing about *what* the caller wants — that's the test's scenario. The same persona calls about many different things.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:64:Every project carries one active **default persona** — a project choice, not a persona type. A new project points at Egma's shared default persona. A project may point at any active Egma-provided or Custom persona available to it instead. A default cannot be archived until the project pointer moves. A test created naming no callers receives this pointer, so authoring a first test never waits on authoring a caller.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:68:> Renamed from `digital human` on 2026-08-05 (public issue #8). `digital human` was originally chosen over `persona` for saying plainly that the caller is synthetic — accepting that users arriving from other tools would say "persona" and need correcting. They did say it, and the correcting bought nothing: `persona` is the voice industry's near-unanimous term, and now it is egma's. Also considered and still not chosen: `simulant`, `virtual human`, `synthetic user`, `phantom`, `surrogate`.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:75:- **personas** — an array. One to start; several when a scenario should be checked against several kinds of caller. Three personas on a test means running it produces three simulations.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:85:**mock tool** — a project-owned stand-in for one of the agent's tools: the tool's name, and the answer egma serves when the agent calls it during a simulation. The answer may be an error — that is how a test forces the failure branch — and may carry a delay, so a mocked backend takes as long as the real one would. **Matching is by tool name, strictly: one answer per tool.** A mock tool never reads a call's arguments; wrong arguments are caught by grading, not matching, because the arguments are on the record either way. Chosen over `tool mock` because it is the word users arrive with (Cekura, Vapi) — the persona lesson, applied the cheap way this time. Added 2026-08-09, mock-tools grilling.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:97:**A run pins the versions it executed against** through its evidence records, not through a versioned suite. Each simulation pins its exact test and persona versions, and the run's grading plan pins its exact grader versions. Editing any of them cannot rewrite what last week's result meant. **Authored things are never overwritten**: an edit creates a new version and the old one remains. Mock tools are the single exception — unversioned by decision, and held to one world per run by snapshot rather than by version, for the reasons the Mock tools section gives. The run row itself keeps the stable suite ID and no second pinned-test list. See [ADR-0013](docs/adr/0013-test-suites-are-containers.md) and [The Postgres control-plane schema](.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/08-postgres-control-plane-schema.md).
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:101:A run produces one simulation per test per persona. Running the same test twice produces two simulations — there is no separate word for a repeat.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:105:**simulator** — the component that executes a simulation: it brings the persona to life, holds the conversation with the agent over a connection, and emits the transcript, outcome, metrics and spans. It runs inside egma's own deployment, hosted or self-hosted — never anywhere else. Earlier records call it *the runtime* or *the simulation runtime*; `simulator` is the canonical name, adopted 2026-08-03 when the simulator effort began.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:123:**metric** — something **measured**, not judged: duration, turn count, latency percentiles, interruption count, tool-call count, cost. **Derived from the trace's spans by one shared measure module** — the same computation serves the metrics display and the graders, for simulations and production traces alike, so the number on screen and the number judged can never disagree. (Previously *emitted by the runtime*; re-homed to spans 2026-08-14, grader-redesign grilling — the simulator's duty is emitting honest span timings.) Never an entity, never attached to a test.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:135:**grader** — a running copy of a grader-library entry: the row that judges, and the thing verdict rows name. Created by pressing **Use** on a library entry, or seeded at project creation. It points at its entry (`library_id` — the connecting tissue, never null, never orphaned: deleting a referenced entry is refused), carries the entry's `type`, and holds its **filled-in values** — latency's `[{metric, bound}]` — in immutable versions; editing the values mints the next version, and a run pins the versions it executed. Each grader version also points at one immutable grader-library definition version. The prompt or code is shared once at the library layer, never copied into each project, while the exact definition used by an old run stays reconstructable. Redefined 2026-08-19, model-execution cutover; the word previously named the authored logic itself.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:147:**grader library** — the shelf of grader definitions: `grader_library` holds each stable library identity and immutable definition versions hold its executable prompt, output definition, parameter schema, or code. An entry declares its **type** — `llm_as_judge` or `code`; reserved: `human`, `ml_model`, `external`. **Owner derives from tenancy**: null organization and project means egma owns the entry — the one deliberate exception to hard-required tenancy — seeded from a catalog in egma's code. When an Egma release changes a definition, reconciliation mints one new shared definition version and new grader versions for active running copies. New runs pin those versions; old runs keep the old definition through their already-pinned grader versions. No definition is copied per project, and no catalog edit changes the meaning of an old verdict. Team-authored entries land in the same library with tenancy set, when custom authoring arrives. Redefined 2026-08-19, model-execution cutover.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:149:**predefined grader** — a library entry egma owns and ships. v0 ships two: **expected_behaviors** (`llm_as_judge`) and **latency** (`code`). Replaces *built-in grader*, 2026-08-14 — `predefined` is the word users arrive with (Cekura), the persona lesson applied the cheap way again.
egma-planning/CONTEXT.md:173:**pull / push** — the explicit sync verbs between the egma folder and the platform, on git's model: `pull` writes the platform's current versions into files; `push` uploads and **refuses** when the platform has moved since the last pull. **That refusal is a property of versioned things**: a test earns it, and so do the mock-tool overrides that version with it. A project mock tool is unversioned by decision, so it has no version to have moved — pushing `egma/mock-tools.md` is last-write-wins, and a teammate's edit in between is not detected; the run's snapshot and the answers on the record carry that history instead. Sync is always a verb a developer runs, never a background process — two silently-syncing authoring surfaces are the documented failure (Humanloop's copy-drift).

egma-planning/docs/adr/0011-one-versioned-platform-api.md:6:Egma's web app, CLI, and outside clients all act on the same organizations, projects, agents, connections, tests, runs, simulations, personas, graders, and verdicts. They use one customer-facing platform API under `/v1`, rather than separate first-party `/api/*` routes and public routes. One executable definition of each operation owns its method, path, request, response, refusals, and authentication choices; it drives server validation and serialization, the OpenAPI document, and one generated TypeScript client.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0011-one-versioned-platform-api.md:8:The platform API covers customer-managed Egma resources, including members, invitation management, API keys, monitoring sources, monitoring import failures, trace reads, and recording access. Identity flows, deployment-wide settings, simulator work traffic, OTLP ingestion, and health checks remain separate protocols. Platform resource paths are organization-wide: a project is a write field and an optional read filter, never a path parent. This cutover changes the contract seam, not the product model: existing resource addresses and operation behavior remain intact after the `/api` prefix becomes `/v1`.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0011-one-versioned-platform-api.md:16:The first `/v1` release preserves the behavior of every current platform operation. This includes atomic agent registration and provider reuse, later connection creation, archive and restore actions, saved test-to-agent applicability, and the current run-selection rules. Those behaviors can change only in a later focused product-model change that updates the contract, server, callers, and tests together. Stable server-owned catalogs remain platform operations in their current form; a screen's private form layout does not become a new resource as part of this cutover.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0011-one-versioned-platform-api.md:18:The platform API is explicit rather than inferred from every Fastify route or every path beginning with `/v1`. Better Auth and Egma's current account and device-login routes stay outside its OpenAPI document. Egma does not add a separate versioned auth contract until a real public account-lifecycle client needs one. Private simulator claim, heartbeat, and report traffic also remains separate. `POST /v1/traces` remains OTLP and is excluded even though platform trace reads use `GET` at the same path; `/health` remains unversioned.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0011-one-versioned-platform-api.md:28:- **Keep one internal first-party contract and add a second public contract.** Rejected because both contracts would model the same platform resources and would drift.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0011-one-versioned-platform-api.md:29:- **Redesign resources while introducing `/v1`.** Rejected b…250 tokens truncated…ocks; it wraps exactly those. A wrapped call goes to egma before anything real runs, so a mocked tool's real implementation is never touched. A tool no mock covers runs natively — untouched and unobserved. (Revised 2026-08-09, same session: the first design wrapped every tool so real calls were observed and stamped `pass-through`; the founder cut the receipt — wrapping only what egma answers is simpler, and the record stays honest at the tool grain via discovery.) The simulator's room driver registers the RPC handlers and serves answers from the claimed spec's resolved mock tools — snapshotted at run creation — delaying each answer by the mock's declared delay.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0008-mock-tools-are-served-over-in-room-rpc.md:23:> **Amended 2026-08-10.** What the SDK actually reads is the identity in dispatch metadata, and one shape of a livekit connection never writes any: on the token-endpoint mode the customer's endpoint dispatches their agent, not egma, so egma is in the room and the agent is never told so. egma-planning/docs/adr/0013-test-suites-are-containers.md:7:Egma defines a test suite as an unversioned, named container inside a project, with every test in exactly one suite. This replaces the earlier saved-selector model, which correctly protected test reuse and suite-independent verdicts but incorrectly treated overlapping execution selection as proof that tests need no primary home. Suites never carry graders, targets, or execution settings. A project grader may refer to a stable suite ID from its own scope; that reference selects container membership without moving grader policy onto the suite.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0013-test-suites-are-containers.md:23:A run keeps the stable ID of the suite that started it. It does not copy the suite name, copy its membership, mint a suite version, or store a membership revision or fingerprint. A later rename is visible on old run pages because the ID still names the same suite. Run creation resolves the suite and creates every simulation with the exact test and persona versions it will execute in one transaction. Those simulation records are the execution plan and the evidence; the run row carries no second list of pinned test versions. This is not a version or snapshot of the suite.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0013-test-suites-are-containers.md:65:After that migration, every test requires one immutable suite ID. Do not add nullable transitional membership, compatibility aliases, old API fields or endpoints, dual reads or writes, ongoing backfills, name-based fallback, or legacy/default-suite behavior. Do not preserve the `test_agent` relationship or its filters. The current suite-name-to-run-label behavior is removed. The migration itself is the complete old-data path; product code implements only the new model.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0007-grading-runs-in-its-own-service.md:8:Verdicts have to come from somewhere, and three homes were on the table. Inside the simulator, at hang-up: lowest conceivable latency for simulations — but production traces never pass through a simulator, so a second grading path would exist from day one; judge-model credentials would spread into simulator configuration; and a capacity slot would be held hostage to judge-model latency on every conversation. Inside the control-plane API process: no new deployable — but grading is bursty in a way a request path is not (one run of thirty-six simulations with five behaviors each lands ~180 judge calls at once), and production grading adds a steady stream scaled by the customer's call volume, not by egma's request rate. Or its own service.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0007-grading-runs-in-its-own-service.md:10:Two prior decisions bear on this. ADR-0004 left "how the built-in expected-behaviors grader executes" to the simulator effort — written when the simulator seemed the natural home. And ADR-0005 settled the dispatch shape for egma's standing workers: pull-based claims, outbound-only arrows, zero inbound surface — proven by the simulator in production shape.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0007-grading-runs-in-its-own-service.md:12:The latency requirement that drove the in-simulator temptation turned out not to need it: the simulator posts its terminal transition within milliseconds of hang-up, deterministic graders execute in-process instantly, and parallel judge calls make wall-clock ≈ one model call regardless of behavior count. The judge model dominates wherever grading runs.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0007-grading-runs-in-its-own-service.md:18:**The simulator stays judge-free** and releases its capacity slot at hang-up. **The API process stays free of judge fan-out**; it keeps the grader factory's CRUD and the read surface.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0007-grading-runs-in-its-own-service.md:25:- Judge credentials live only in the control plane's credential store; the simulator's configuration surface does not grow.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-simulation-runtime-is-pipecat-in-python.md:1:# The simulation runtime is Pipecat, in Python, quarantined behind the simulation contract
egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-simulation-runtime-is-pipecat-in-python.md:3:The simulation runtime — the service that plays the persona and conducts simulations — is built on Pipecat and is therefore Python, inside an otherwise all-TypeScript monorepo. Ticket 10 already said "most likely Pipecat"; this record firms it up and adds the reasoning that survived a fresh comparison (2026-08-05).
egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-simulation-runtime-is-pipecat-in-python.md:5:egma's runtime is a *caller into other people's infrastructure*: it must join a Retell session, speak a telephony provider's media protocol, or attach to whatever transport a future connection type demands. Pipecat is a transport-agnostic pipeline whose exposed frame/processor model makes testing instrumentation — per-turn latency stamps, dual-channel recording, scripted interruptions, injected noise, the measured audio band ticket 10 made irreversible — ordinary middleware rather than a fork. The alternatives: LiveKit Agents assumes it owns the media (agents live in LiveKit rooms, adding a LiveKit server + SIP service to every self-hosted deployment) — the right shape for *hosting* agents, not *visiting* them — and its Node SDK, the one TypeScript path anywhere, officially trails its Python SDK. Pipecat has no server-side TypeScript at all, so choosing it is choosing Python.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-simulation-runtime-is-pipecat-in-python.md:9:If LiveKit's SIP stack ever becomes the right telephony backbone, it joins as a transport under Pipecat or as a new connection type; adopting it does not reopen this decision. Licensing per ticket 10: Pipecat BSD-2-Clause, LiveKit Apache-2.0, both compatible — re-check when they land in the build.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-implicit-expected-behaviors-grader.md:8:The domain model required every test to name **at least one grader at write time** — a test with no graders is unfalsifiable, and a suite of unfalsifiable tests is a wall of green that could never have been red, which is the exact false trust this product exists to kill. The rule was sound; its enforcement was impossible. The test factory was ready to build and graders did not exist: no table, no factory, nothing for a test to name. Building a minimal grader entity first would have front-run fog the map deliberately left unresolved (*what a grader is made of* is explicitly unspecified), and sequencing a grader effort ahead of tests would have delayed the simulator's critical path.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-implicit-expected-behaviors-grader.md:20:**How the built-in executes** — prompt shape, per-behavior verdicts, what it reads beyond the transcript — is the simulator effort's decision, deliberately not made here.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-implicit-expected-behaviors-grader.md:24:- The test factory ships with no grader scaffolding and no dependency on a grader effort; the simulator's critical path shortens by one entity.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-implicit-expected-behaviors-grader.md:25:- Every test is falsifiable from birth, and the day the simulator runs its first simulation there is already a judge — no window where results exist but verdicts don't.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0004-implicit-expected-behaviors-grader.md:27:- The control-plane spec's write-time rejection story ("a test with no graders is rejected") is superseded in place by behaviors-empty rejection; the domain model's test definition and Judging section are edited accordingly, and **built-in grader** / **expected-behaviors grader** enter the glossary.

egma-planning/docs/adr/0009-the-cli-and-the-platform-ship-together.md:16:Ticket 08 makes the coupling tighter rather than looser. The repository file format now records a behavior's priority, a persona's stable identifier, a test's description, its graders, its required capabilities, and the identity revision of its live half. A CLI that cannot read those cannot write a correct file, and a platform that cannot answer them cannot be written to correctly.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0009-the-cli-and-the-platform-ship-together.md:25:- The number is bumped whenever a shape a repository client reads or writes changes. Contract **2** was: behaviors carry a priority, personas carry a stable identifier beside their display name, a test carries a description, graders, required capabilities and an identity revision, and a repository write names both the version and the revision it was written against.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0009-the-cli-and-the-platform-ship-together.md:26:- **Contract 3 is the current one, and it is the first bump this decision was written to absorb.** The grader redesign ([ADR-0009 on graders](0009-grader-library-and-running-copies.md), 2026-08-14) retired the two fields contract 2 was mostly defined by: an expected behavior is a plain sentence again, because under binary scoring every behavior must hold and a priority had nothing left to say; and a test names no graders, because the project's running copies judge every test and the junction is dropped. Contract 3 is contract 2 without those two — a persona's stable identifier, a test's description, its required capabilities, its identity revision, and a write naming both the version and the revision. On read, a contract-2 file is tolerated rather than refused: the `[P0]` markers and the `graders:` key are passed over and the file is rewritten as contract 3. That tolerance is deliberate and it is the one place this decision bends, because refusing would strand a folder somebody committed months ago over fields the platform has stopped having an opinion about.
egma-planning/docs/adr/0014-object-storage-is-the-trace-ingestion-boundary.md:6:Egma is pre-production, so this is one forward replacement rather than a compatibility migration. The existing OTLP wire contract and `POST /v1/traces` URL remain unchanged. Customer production OTLP and simulator service-token OTLP use the same ingestion path; Retell enters it through the same internal acceptance module. Egma authenticates, validates, and normalizes accepted evidence, appends the versioned normalized envelope to a bounded local staging write-ahead log, and groups those records into immutable segments. It uploads each segment to the configured object store: AWS S3 for hosted Egma and MinIO for self-hosted Egma.

Request authorization, the simulator service token, configured Retell key, and object-store credentials stay outside evidence by construction. egma-planning/docs/adr/0001-auth-provider-owns-identity-only.md:11:BetterAuth ships an organization plugin (organization → team → member, with roles and invitations) and an API-key plugin. egma-planning/docs/adr/0001-auth-provider-owns-identity-only.md:72:So a swap needs **no data migration and no re-modelling**. Nothing is exported from a vendor, nothing is re-keyed, no row moves. That was the half that could have cost a quarter, and it is safe. Nothing below takes it back.

**production ingestion** — how egma receives evidence of real production conversations. It is separate from a simulation connection. An agent platform may have platform-specific ingestion strategies, such as polling Retell's calls API or receiving LiveKit spans through OTLP. Production-ingestion ownership and configuration are settled by their own design, not inferred from a connection kind or access variant. Added 2026-08-19 during the production-monitoring grilling.

**monitoring setup** — the customer configuration that lets egma receive production evidence from one agent platform. Setup starts by selecting the agent platform and then follows that platform's required steps; one setup may select several agents reported by that platform. The platform-specific production-ingestion process runs from this setup. A monitoring setup is not a simulation connection. Added 2026-08-19 during the production-monitoring grilling.

**A simulation records the connection it ran over, and this is load-bearing.** 8 kHz μ-law and WebRTC produce *different units*: the codec destroys information audio graders need and inflates every latency number. Comparing scores across connection types is invalid. See [How to connect to a voice agent, per framework](.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/04-voice-agent-connection-per-framework.md).

## The caller

**persona** — the synthetic person who calls the agent. Who they are: manner, patience, accent, background noise, and how they behave under friction. A first-class, reusable, versioned entity. A persona is either **Egma-provided** and shared read-only, or **Custom** and owned by one project.

**persona version** — one immutable, executable form of a persona. It owns the caller's traits and the complete model selection used to bring that caller to life: LLM provider and model, STT provider and model, and TTS provider, model, voice ID, and speed. The technical voice has no second home in traits or platform settings. Editing any of these facts creates a new persona version.

A persona says nothing about *what* the caller wants — that's the test's scenario. The same persona calls about many different things.

Every project carries one active **default persona** — a project choice, not a persona type. A new project points at Egma's shared default persona. A project may point at any active Egma-provided or Custom persona available to it instead. A default cannot be archived until the project pointer moves. A test created naming no callers receives this pointer, so authoring a first test never waits on authoring a caller.

In a transcript the two speakers are labelled **`human:`** and **`agent:`**.

> Renamed from `digital human` on 2026-08-05 (public issue #8). `digital human` was originally chosen over `persona` for saying plainly that the caller is synthetic — accepting that users arriving from other tools would say "persona" and need correcting. They did say it, and the correcting bought nothing: `persona` is the voice industry's near-unanimous term, and now it is egma's. Also considered and still not chosen: `simulant`, `virtual human`, `synthetic user`, `phantom`, `surrogate`.

## The specification

**test** — one authored specification. Anthropic's *task*. Owned by the project and contained by exactly one test suite. It never belongs or applies to named agents. It holds:

**A run pins the versions it executed against** through its evidence records, not through a versioned suite. Each simulation pins its exact test and persona versions, and the run's grading plan pins its exact grader versions. Editing any of them cannot rewrite what last week's result meant. **Authored things are never overwritten**: an edit creates a new version and the old one remains. Mock tools are the single exception — unversioned by decision, and held to one world per run by snapshot rather than by version, for the reasons the Mock tools section gives. The run row itself keeps the stable suite ID and no second pinned-test list. See [ADR-0013](docs/adr/0013-test-suites-are-containers.md) and [The Postgres control-plane schema](.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/08-postgres-control-plane-schema.md).

**simulation** — one test executed once, inside a run. One conversation, start to finish. Anthropic's *trial*.

A run produces one simulation per test per persona. Running the same test twice produces two simulations — there is no separate word for a repeat.

Every simulation produces a transcript, an outcome, metrics, and grades.

**simulator** — the component that executes a simulation: it brings the persona to life, holds the conversation with the agent over a connection, and emits the transcript, outcome, metrics and spans. It runs inside egma's own deployment, hosted or self-hosted — never anywhere else. Earlier records call it *the runtime* or *the simulation runtime*; `simulator` is the canonical name, adopted 2026-08-03 when the simulator effort began.

## Production monitoring

**monitoring source** — a project-owned source of production calls from an agent platform. It holds what egma needs to find and import calls from the selected production targets.

**monitoring import failure** — one production call that a monitoring source could not import after its allowed attempts. It remains visible so a user can inspect the failure and retry the import.

# The simulation runtime is Pipecat, in Python, quarantined behind the simulation contract

The simulation runtime — the service that plays the persona and conducts simulations — is built on Pipecat and is therefore Python, inside an otherwise all-TypeScript monorepo. Ticket 10 already said "most likely Pipecat"; this record firms it up and adds the reasoning that survived a fresh comparison (2026-08-05).

egma's runtime is a *caller into other people's infrastructure*: it must join a Retell session, speak a telephony provider's media protocol, or attach to whatever transport a future connection type demands. Pipecat is a transport-agnostic pipeline whose exposed frame/processor model makes testing instrumentation — per-turn latency stamps, dual-channel recording, scripted interruptions, injected noise, the measured audio band ticket 10 made irreversible — ordinary middleware rather than a fork. The alternatives: LiveKit Agents assumes it owns the media (agents live in LiveKit rooms, adding a LiveKit server + SIP service to every self-hosted deployment) — the right shape for *hosting* agents, not *visiting* them — and its Node SDK, the one TypeScript path anywhere, officially trails its Python SDK. Pipecat has no server-side TypeScript at all, so choosing it is choosing Python.

The language cost is contained by a boundary that exists for its own reasons: the runtime receives fully-resolved simulation specs and reports over a language-neutral HTTP contract, never touches Postgres, never imports monorepo code. The contract is the language firewall.

If LiveKit's SIP stack ever becomes the right telephony backbone, it joins as a transport under Pipecat or as a new connection type; adopting it does not reopen this decision. Licensing per ticket 10: Pipecat BSD-2-Clause, LiveKit Apache-2.0, both compatible — re-check when they land in the build.
# ADR-0010: Persona versions own model execution

Status: accepted — 2026-08-19

## Context

Production assembled one simulation from unrelated live settings. Postgres held STT provider `openai` from an older deployment and later inserted model `gpt-live-transcribe` into an empty row. Readiness checked that values existed, not that they formed a valid selection. The simulator therefore sent a realtime-only model to the completed-audio endpoint and failed before turn one.

The same design also gave technical voice two owners: persona traits and platform speech settings. A run pinned the persona version but claim assembly read model and speech settings again later. An old result therefore did not have one immutable meaning.

## Decision

One persona version owns one complete execution selection:

- traits contain human behavior only;
- `models.llm` contains provider and model;
- `models.stt` contains provider and model;
- `models.tts` contains provider, model, voice ID, and speed.

`models` is required. There is no nullable or legacy execution path. A one-time pre-launch migration gives every existing version one complete validated selection and removes technical voice from traits.

A model-judged grader version owns its own required LLM provider and model
selection. A code grader owns no model because it makes no model call.

Provider credentials are operational data and never belong to a persona,
grader, run, or platform-setting row. For Egma Cloud, the credential owner is
Egma and the simulator and grader call providers directly. The API reads the
current AWS bundle while assembling a simulation claim and puts only the
selected providers' keys in that complete work order. The grader reads the
bundle itself only after a claimed job resolves at least one model-judged
grader. For self-hosted Egma, the API and grader use the operator-supplied
provider keys through the same custody interface. Self-hosted use of
Egma-owned credentials is unavailable until a gateway is built.

The first release has no gateway, no Cloud BYOK mode, no organization model-access switch, and no fallback. A selected provider without a current credential fails before execution with one direct error.

The run pins the persona and grader version IDs. It does not own credentials or network routes.

## Consequences

- Provider, model, voice, and speed cannot drift within a pinned persona version.
- On Egma Cloud, credential rotation affects the next simulation claim and the
  next model-judged grading job without minting a persona version or restarting
  a worker. A self-hosted deployment that supplies keys through container
  environment variables must recreate the API and grader containers after
  changing them.
- AWS Secrets Manager stores secret values only. It does not select models or voices.
- Postgres platform settings keep platform operations such as the phone route. They stop owning model, speech, VAD, media, or provider-key choices.
- The simulator receives one complete validated execution document. It does not fill missing model fields from container defaults.
- The persona library and Custom personas use the same version shape. Fork copies traits and models in one transaction.
- A later gateway adds one transport for self-hosted use of Egma credentials. It does not change persona, grader, or credential ownership.

## Rejected alternatives

- Per-field insert-only platform settings: this caused the production hybrid.
- Nullable `persona_version.models` with a fallback: this preserves the same failure class.
- Technical voice in both traits and models: two owners can disagree.
- Gateway for Egma Cloud: Egma already controls both worker and credential, so the extra hop adds latency and another failure point.
- Provider keys in a run snapshot: rotation is operational state, not authored meaning.

# ADR-0010: Persona versions own model execution

Status: accepted — 2026-08-19

## Context

Production assembled one simulation from unrelated live settings. Postgres held STT provider `openai` from an older deployment and later inserted model `gpt-live-transcribe` into an empty row. Readiness checked that values existed, not that they formed a valid selection. The simulator therefore sent a realtime-only model to the completed-audio endpoint and failed before turn one.

The same design also gave technical voice two owners: persona traits and platform speech settings. A run pinned the persona version but claim assembly read model and speech settings again later. An old result therefore did not have one immutable meaning.

## Decision

One persona version owns one complete execution selection:

- traits contain human behavior only;
- `models.llm` contains provider and model;
- `models.stt` contains provider and model;
- `models.tts` contains provider, model, voice ID, and speed.

`models` is required. There is no nullable or legacy execution path. A one-time pre-launch migration gives every existing version one complete validated selection and removes technical voice from traits.

A model-judged grader version owns its own required LLM provider and model
selection. A code grader owns no model because it makes no model call.

Provider credentials are operational data and never belong to a persona,
grader, run, or platform-setting row. For Egma Cloud, the credential owner is
Egma and the simulator and grader call providers directly. The API reads the
current AWS bundle while assembling a simulation claim and puts only the
selected providers' keys in that complete work order. The grader reads the
bundle itself only after a claimed job resolves at least one model-judged
grader. For self-hosted Egma, the API and grader use the operator-supplied
provider keys through the same custody interface. Self-hosted use of
Egma-owned credentials is unavailable until a gateway is built.

The first release has no gateway, no Cloud BYOK mode, no organization model-access switch, and no fallback. A selected provider without a current credential fails before execution with one direct error.

The run pins the persona and grader version IDs. It does not own credentials or network routes.

## Consequences

- Provider, model, voice, and speed cannot drift within a pinned persona version.
- On Egma Cloud, credential rotation affects the next simulation claim and the
  next model-judged grading job without minting a persona version or restarting
  a worker. A self-hosted deployment that supplies keys through container
  environment variables must recreate the API and grader containers after
  changing them.
- AWS Secrets Manager stores secret values only. It does not select models or voices.
- Postgres platform settings keep platform operations such as the phone route. They stop owning model, speech, VAD, media, or provider-key choices.
- The simulator receives one complete validated execution document. It does not fill missing model fields from container defaults.
- The persona library and Custom personas use the same version shape. Fork copies traits and models in one transaction.
- A later gateway adds one transport for self-hosted use of Egma credentials. It does not change persona, grader, or credential ownership.

## Rejected alternatives

- Per-field insert-only platform settings: this caused the production hybrid.
- Nullable `persona_version.models` with a fallback: this preserves the same failure class.
- Technical voice in both traits and models: two owners can disagree.
- Gateway for Egma Cloud: Egma already controls both worker and credential, so the extra hop adds latency and another failure point.
- Provider keys in a run snapshot: rotation is operational state, not authored meaning.

**production ingestion** — how egma receives evidence of real production conversations. It is separate from a simulation connection. An agent platform may have platform-specific ingestion strategies, such as polling Retell's calls API or receiving LiveKit spans through OTLP. Production-ingestion ownership and configuration are settled by their own design, not inferred from a connection kind or access variant. Added 2026-08-19 during the production-monitoring grilling.

**monitoring setup** — the customer configuration that lets egma receive production evidence from one agent platform. Setup starts by selecting the agent platform and then follows that platform's required steps; one setup may select several agents reported by that platform. The platform-specific production-ingestion process runs from this setup. A monitoring setup is not a simulation connection. Added 2026-08-19 during the production-monitoring grilling.

**A simulation records the connection it ran over, and this is load-bearing.** 8 kHz μ-law and WebRTC produce *different units*: the codec destroys information audio graders need and inflates every latency number. Comparing scores across connection types is invalid. See [How to connect to a voice agent, per framework](.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/04-voice-agent-connection-per-framework.md).

## The caller

**persona** — the synthetic person who calls the agent. Who they are: manner, patience, accent, background noise, and how they behave under friction. A first-class, reusable, versioned entity. A persona is either **Egma-provided** and shared read-only, or **Custom** and owned by one project.

**persona version** — one immutable, executable form of a persona. It owns the caller's traits and the complete model selection used to bring that caller to life: LLM provider and model, STT provider and model, and TTS provider, model, voice ID, and speed. The technical voice has no second home in traits or platform settings. Editing any of these facts creates a new persona version.

A persona says nothing about *what* the caller wants — that's the test's scenario. The same persona calls about many different things.

Every project carries one active **default persona** — a project choice, not a persona type. A new project points at Egma's shared default persona. A project may point at any active Egma-provided or Custom persona available to it instead. A default cannot be archived until the project pointer moves. A test created naming no callers receives this pointer, so authoring a first test never waits on authoring a caller.

In a transcript the two speakers are labelled **`human:`** and **`agent:`**.

> Renamed from `digital human` on 2026-08-05 (public issue #8). `digital human` was originally chosen over `persona` for saying plainly that the caller is synthetic — accepting that users arriving from other tools would say "persona" and need correcting. They did say it, and the correcting bought nothing: `persona` is the voice industry's near-unanimous term, and now it is egma's. Also considered and still not chosen: `simulant`, `virtual human`, `synthetic user`, `phantom`, `surrogate`.

## The specification

**test** — one authored specification. Anthropic's *task*. Owned by the project and contained by exactly one test suite. It never belongs or applies to named agents. It holds:

**A run pins the versions it executed against** through its evidence records, not through a versioned suite. Each simulation pins its exact test and persona versions, and the run's grading plan pins its exact grader versions. Editing any of them cannot rewrite what last week's result meant. **Authored things are never overwritten**: an edit creates a new version and the old one remains. Mock tools are the single exception — unversioned by decision, and held to one world per run by snapshot rather than by version, for the reasons the Mock tools section gives. The run row itself keeps the stable suite ID and no second pinned-test list. See [ADR-0013](docs/adr/0013-test-suites-are-containers.md) and [The Postgres control-plane schema](.scratch/first-simulation-path/issues/08-postgres-control-plane-schema.md).

**simulation** — one test executed once, inside a run. One conversation, start to finish. Anthropic's *trial*.

A run produces one simulation per test per persona. Running the same test twice produces two simulations — there is no separate word for a repeat.

Every simulation produces a transcript, an outcome, metrics, and grades.

**simulator** — the component that executes a simulation: it brings the persona to life, holds the conversation with the agent over a connection, and emits the transcript, outcome, metrics and spans. It runs inside egma's own deployment, hosted or self-hosted — never anywhere else. Earlier records call it *the runtime* or *the simulation runtime*; `simulator` is the canonical name, adopted 2026-08-03 when the simulator effort began.

## Production monitoring

**monitoring source** — a project-owned source of production calls from an agent platform. It holds what egma needs to find and import calls from the selected production targets.

**monitoring import failure** — one production call that a monitoring source could not import after its allowed attempts. It remains visible so a user can inspect the failure and retry the import.

# The simulation runtime is Pipecat, in Python, quarantined behind the simulation contract

The simulation runtime — the service that plays the persona and conducts simulations — is built on Pipecat and is therefore Python, inside an otherwise all-TypeScript monorepo. Ticket 10 already said "most likely Pipecat"; this record firms it up and adds the reasoning that survived a fresh comparison (2026-08-05).

egma's runtime is a *caller into other people's infrastructure*: it must join a Retell session, speak a telephony provider's media protocol, or attach to whatever transport a future connection type demands. Pipecat is a transport-agnostic pipeline whose exposed frame/processor model makes testing instrumentation — per-turn latency stamps, dual-channel recording, scripted interruptions, injected noise, the measured audio band ticket 10 made irreversible — ordinary middleware rather than a fork. The alternatives: LiveKit Agents assumes it owns the media (agents live in LiveKit rooms, adding a LiveKit server + SIP service to every self-hosted deployment) — the right shape for *hosting* agents, not *visiting* them — and its Node SDK, the one TypeScript path anywhere, officially trails its Python SDK. 1	"""The persona brain: one component, shared by every modality forever.
     2	
     3	It composes the persona's authored human traits and the test's scenario into a
     4	system prompt, takes turns — the transcript's ``human`` side — and decides
     5	when the exchange is concluded. What it does not know is deliberate: it
     6	never sees a platform (that is the plug's business) and never produces its
     7	own words (that is the model client's), so the same brain conducts a chat
     8	today and speaks through voice legs when those arrive.
     9	
    10	Role mapping is from the persona's own seat at the table: the persona is
    11	the ``assistant`` the model plays, and the agent under test is the
    12	``user`` it is answering.
    13	"""
    14	
    15	from __future__ import annotations
    16	
    17	import json
    18	from collections.abc import Sequence
    19	from dataclasses import dataclass
    20	from typing import Any
    21	
    22	from .model import CONCLUDE_MARKER, ModelClient, PersonaReply
    23	
    24	OPENING_NUDGE = (
    25	    "(The conversation is open and the agent is listening. Speak your first turn.)"
    26	)
    27	"""Stands in for the silence when the persona goes first: chat-shaped
    28	models answer a user message, and an empty history has none to answer."""
    29	
    30	_PROMPT_FRAME = """\
    31	You are playing a persona to test an AI voice agent.
    32	
    33	Who you are, exactly as authored:
    34	
    35	{traits}
    36	
    37	Why you are here today:
    38	
    39	{scenario}
    40	
    41	How to conduct yourself:
    42	- Stay in character as this person for the whole exchange. Never mention \
    43	being simulated, tested, or an AI.
    44	- Speak one conversational turn at a time, in plain spoken words — no \
    45	lists, no headings, no stage directions.
    46	- Pursue what you came for until it is concluded to your satisfaction, \
    47	and let your persona decide how patiently.
    48	- When your goal is concluded and nothing further is needed, say a brief \
    49	goodbye and end your reply with {marker}.
    50	"""
    51	
    52	
    53	def compose_system_prompt(traits: dict[str, Any], scenario_instructions: str) -> str:
    54	    """Human traits and scenario, composed into the persona's instructions.
    55	
    56	    Contract v3 admits the complete human-traits value and excludes technical
    57	    voice. Render that complete value so every authored human fact reaches the
    58	    model, without a model or deployment fallback.
    59	    """
    60	    return _PROMPT_FRAME.format(
    61	        traits=json.dumps(traits, indent=2, sort_keys=True),
    62	        scenario=scenario_instructions,
    63	        marker=CONCLUDE_MARKER,
    64	    )
    65	
    66	
    67	@dataclass(frozen=True)
    68	class Turn:
    69	    """One transcript turn: who spoke (``human`` or ``agent``), and what."""
    70	
    71	    speaker: str
    72	    text: str
    73	
    74	
    75	def messages_for(system_prompt: str, history: Sequence[Turn]) -> list[dict[str, str]]:
    76	    """The conversation so far, in chat shape, from the persona's seat."""
    77	    messages = [{"role": "system", "content": system_prompt}]
    78	    for turn in history:
    79	        role = "assistant" if turn.speaker == "human" else "user"
    80	        messages.append({"role": role, "content": turn.text})
    81	    if not history:
    82	        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": OPENING_NUDGE})
    83	    return messages
    84

    86	class Persona:
    87	    """The synthetic person on the human side of the transcript."""
    88	
    89	    def __init__(
    90	        self,
    91	        *,
    92	        traits: dict[str, Any],
    93	        scenario_instructions: str,
    94	        model: ModelClient,
    95	    ) -> None:
    96	        self._system_prompt = compose_system_prompt(traits, scenario_instructions)
    97	        self._model = model
    98

   100	    def model_name(self) -> str:

   118	class OpenAICompatibleModel:
   119	    """The direct OpenAI adapter behind the model-client seam.
   120	
   121	    The pinned persona version supplies the model and the claim supplies the
   122	    current key. CI never selects this client.
   123	    """
   124	
   125	    def __init__(
   126	        self,
   127	        *,
   128	        base_url: str,
   129	        api_key: str,
   130	        model_name: str,
   131	        timeout_seconds: float = MODEL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS,
   132	    ) -> None:
   133	        self._base_url = base_url.rstrip("/")
   134	        self._api_key = api_key
   135	        self._model_name = model_name
   136	        self._timeout = aiohttp.ClientTimeout(total=timeout_seconds)
   137	        self._session: aiohttp.ClientSession | None = None
   138	
   139	    @property
   140	    def model_name(self) -> str:
   141	        return self._model_name
   142	
   143	    def _live_session(self) -> aiohttp.ClientSession:
   144	        if self._session is None:
   145	            self._session = aiohttp.ClientSession()
   146	        return self._session
   147	
   148	    def _provider_detail(self, value: object) -> str:
   149	        """A bounded provider detail with this client's credential removed.
   150	
   151	        Model failures cross Pipecat's traced service seam. Pipecat records
   152	        exception messages on its native span, before the simulation lifecycle
   153	        applies its process-wide redactor, so the client must remove the key at
   154	        the source.
   155	        """
   156	        rendered = value if isinstance(value, str) else repr(value)
   157	        return self._without_api_key(rendered)[:200]
   158	
   159	    def _without_api_key(self, text: str) -> str:
   160	        """Remove this client's bearer key from provider-authored text.
   161	
   162	        A one-character development key such as ``k`` must not rewrite every
   163	        word containing that letter. Short keys are therefore removed when
   164	        they appear as their own token, which still covers an echoed bearer,
   165	        JSON value, URL parameter, or provider sentence. Real provider keys are
   166	        long enough to replace exactly wherever they occur.
   167	        """
   168	        if not self._api_key:
   169	            return text
   170	        if len(self._api_key) >= 8:
   171	            return text.replace(self._api_key, REDACTED)
   172	        return re.sub(
   173	            rf"(?<![{_SHORT_SECRET_CHARS}]){re.escape(self._api_key)}"
   174	            rf"(?![{_SHORT_SECRET_CHARS}])",
   175	            REDACTED,
   176	            text,
   177	        )
   178	
   179	    async def reply(self, messages: list[dict[str, str]]) -> PersonaReply:
   180	        asked = {"model": self._model_name, "messages": messages}
   181	        try:
   182	            async with self._live_session().post(
   183	                f"{self._base_url}/chat/completions",
   184	                json=asked,
   185	                headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {self._api_key}"},
   186	                timeout=self._timeout,
   187	            ) as response:
   188	                if response.status != 200:
   189	                    raise ModelFailure(
   190	                        f"the model answered {response.status}: "
   191	                        f"{self._provider_detail(await response.text())}"
   192	                    )
   193	                body = await response.json()
   194	        except UNREACHABLE as error:
   195	            raise ModelFailure(
   196	                f"the model was unreachable: {self._provider_detail(error)}"
   197	            ) from None
   198	
   199	        try:
   200	            content = body["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]
   201	        except (KeyError, IndexError, TypeError) as unexpected:
   202	            raise ModelFailure(
   203	                "the model's answer had no message content: "
   204	                f"{self._provider_detail(body)}"
   205	            ) from unexpected
   206	        if not isinstance(content, str):
   207	            raise ModelFailure(
   208	                f"the model's content was not text: {self._provider_detail(content)}"
   209	            )

   211	        content = self._without_api_key(content)
   212	        concluded = CONCLUDE_MARKER in content
   213	        text = content.replace(CONCLUDE_MARKER, "").strip()
   214	        if not text:

   218	    async def close(self) -> None:
   219	        if self._session is not None:
   220	            await self._session.close()
   221	            self._session = None

   504	        self, *, service: _PersonaLLMService, conductor: VoiceConductor
   505	    ) -> None:
   506	        super().__init__()
   507	        self._service = service

   514	    async def request(
   515	        self,
   516	        messages: list[dict[str, str]],

   518	        push: Callable[[Frame], Awaitable[None]],
   519	    ) -> None:
   520	        if self._waiting is not None:
   521	            raise RuntimeError("the persona model already has a reply in flight")

   523	        self._waiting = waiting
   524	        self._due = due
   525	        try:
   526	            context = LLMContext(messages=cast(Any, messages))
   527	            await push(LLMContextFrame(context=context))

   529	        except BaseException:
   530	            if self._waiting is waiting:
   531	                self._reset()

   534	    async def process_frame(self, frame: Frame, direction: FrameDirection) -> None:

   537	            await self.push_frame(frame, direction)
   538	            return

   542	            return
   543	        if self._collecting and isinstance(frame, LLMTextFrame):
   544	            self._text.append(frame.text)
   545	            return
   546	        if self._collecting and isinstance(frame, LLMFullResponseEndFrame):
   547	            await self._finish_reply()
   548	            return

   551	    async def _finish_reply(self) -> None:

   554	        assert waiting is not None
   555	        assert due is not None

   557	            reply = self._service.take_reply()

   568	                    )

   122	    current key. CI never selects this client.

   124	
   125	    def __init__(
   126	        self,
   127	        *,
   128	        base_url: str,
   129	        api_key: str,
   130	        model_name: str,
   131	        timeout_seconds: float = MODEL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS,
   132	    ) -> None:
   133	        self._base_url = base_url.rstrip("/")
   134	        self._api_key = api_key
   135	        self._model_name = model_name

   137	        self._session: aiohttp.ClientSession | None = None
   138	
   139	    @property
   140	    def model_name(self) -> str:
   141	        return self._model_name

   143	    def _live_session(self) -> aiohttp.ClientSession:
   144	        if self._session is None:
   145	            self._session = aiohttp.ClientSession()
   146	        return self._session
   147	
   148	    def _provider_detail(self, value: object) -> str:
   149	        """A bounded provider detail with this client's credential removed.
   150	
   151	        Model failures cross Pipecat's traced service seam. Pipecat records
   152	        exception messages on its native span, before the simulation lifecycle
   153	        applies its process-wide redactor, so the client must remove the key at
   154	        the source.
   155	        """
   156	        rendered = value if isinstance(value, str) else repr(value)
   157	        return self._without_api_key(rendered)[:200]
   158	
   159	    def _without_api_key(self, text: str) -> str:
   160	        """Remove this client's bearer key from provider-authored text.
   161	
   162	        A one-character development key such as ``k`` must not rewrite every
   163	        word containing that letter. Short keys are therefore removed when
   164	        they appear as their own token, which still covers an echoed bearer,
   165	        JSON value, URL parameter, or provider sentence. Real provider keys are
   166	        long enough to replace exactly wherever they occur.
   167	        """
   168	        if not self._api_key:
   169	            return text
   170	        if len(self._api_key) >= 8:
   171	            return text.replace(self._api_key, REDACTED)
   172	        return re.sub(
   173	            rf"(?<![{_SHORT_SECRET_CHARS}]){re.escape(self._api_key)}"
   174	            rf"(?![{_SHORT_SECRET_CHARS}])",
   175	            REDACTED,
   176	            text,
   177	        )
   178	
   179	    async def reply(self, messages: list[dict[str, str]]) -> PersonaReply:
   180	        asked = {"model": self._model_name, "messages": messages}
   181	        try:
   182	            async with self._live_session().post(
   183	                f"{self._base_url}/chat/completions",
   184	                json=asked,
   185	                headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {self._api_key}"},
   186	                timeout=self._timeout,
   187	            ) as response:
   188	                if response.status != 200:
   189	                    raise ModelFailure(
   190	                        f"the model answered {response.status}: "
   191	                        f"{self._provider_detail(await response.text())}"
   192	                    )
   193	                body = await response.json()
   194	        except UNREACHABLE as error:
   195	            raise ModelFailure(
   196	                f"the model was unreachable: {self._provider_detail(error)}"
   197	            ) from None
   198	
   199	        try:
   200	            content = body["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]
   201	        except (KeyError, IndexError, TypeError) as unexpected:
   202	            raise ModelFailure(
   203	                "the model's answer had no message content: "
   204	                f"{self._provider_detail(body)}"
   205	            ) from unexpected
   206	        if not isinstance(content, str):
   207	            raise ModelFailure(
   208	                f"the model's content was not text: {self._provider_detail(content)}"
   209	            )
   210	
   211	        content = self._without_api_key(content)

   213	        text = content.replace(CONCLUDE_MARKER, "").strip()
   214	        if not text:
   215	            raise ModelFailure("the model's answer had no words to speak")

   218	    async def close(self) -> None:
   219	        if self._session is not None:
   220	            await self._session.close()
   221	            self._session = None

   436	class _PersonaLLMService(LLMService):
   437	    """Run Egma's existing ModelClient through Pipecat's native LLM seam.
   438	
   439	    Pipecat owns the service lifecycle, instrumentation scope, span, input and
   440	    output attributes. The model client still owns the direct provider request,
   441	    including its non-streaming body and timeout.
   442	    """
   443	
   444	    def __init__(self, *, persona: Persona) -> None:
   445	        super().__init__(
   446	            settings=LLMSettings(
   447	                model=persona.model_name,
   448	                system_instruction=None,
   449	                temperature=None,
   450	                max_tokens=None,
   451	                top_p=None,
   452	                top_k=None,
   453	                frequency_penalty=None,
   454	                presence_penalty=None,
   455	                seed=None,
   456	                filter_incomplete_user_turns=False,
   457	                user_turn_completion_config=None,
   458	            )
   459	        )
   460	        self._persona = persona
   461	        self._reply: PersonaReply | None = None
   462	        self._failure: Exception | None = None
   463	
   464	    @traced_llm
   465	    async def _process_context(self, context: LLMContext) -> None:
   466	        self._reply = None
   467	        self._failure = None
   468	        messages = cast(list[dict[str, str]], context.get_messages())
   469	        reply = await self._persona.reply_to(messages)
   470	        self._reply = reply
   471	        await self.push_frame(LLMTextFrame(reply.text))
   472	
   473	    async def process_frame(self, frame: Frame, direction: FrameDirection) -> None:
   474	        await super().process_frame(frame, direction)
   475	        if isinstance(frame, LLMContextFrame):
   476	            await self.push_frame(LLMFullResponseStartFrame())
   477	            try:
   478	                await self._process_context(frame.context)
   479	            except Exception as fault:
   480	                self._failure = fault
   481	                await self.push_error(
   482	                    "the persona model could not answer", exception=fault
   483	                )
   484	            finally:
   485	                await self.push_frame(LLMFullResponseEndFrame())
   486	            return
   487	        await self.push_frame(frame, direction)
   488	
   489	    def take_reply(self) -> PersonaReply:
   490	        """The reply whose native end frame just reached the gate."""
   491	        failure, self._failure = self._failure, None
   492	        reply, self._reply = self._reply, None
   493	        if failure is not None:
   494	            raise failure
   495	        if reply is None:
   496	            raise RuntimeError("Pipecat ended a persona response with no reply")
   497	        return reply
